subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CATTLE QUOTA FOR THE SECOND QUARTER
speechtext:
On Monday, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) I stated that the quota of cattle exportable to the United States at the reduced rate of duty had not been filled. Yesterday the hon, member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) inquired as to the number of cattle that had been exported from Canada during the present quarter, which began on April 1. At that time I was not able to give him a reply, but to-day I am in a position to give the house some information.
The United States figures available are for the period from April 1 to April 8 inclusive. During this period 11,193 head of cattle, other

than dairy cattle, were exported from Canada at the reduced rate of duty. This represents 2ll-6 per cent of the 51,720 head, which is Canada's share of the quarterly quota of
60,000	head. Our own records give figures for a somewhat longer period, from April 1 to April 13 inclusive. These figures show an export from Canada of 13,288 head of the above class of cattle, shipped to the United States during this period.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle also asked for some information as to the number of head exported from Mexico to the United States. The quota from all countries other than Canada is 8,280 head. On April 1, the first day of the present quarter, there were shipped into the United States 6,940 head, so a very small balance is left for importation from countries other than Canada. I might add that it is understood that practically all the latter number came from Mexico.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, April 18, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Rogers-Mr. Sanderson in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the general interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, and also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, and for the appointment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if it had
been possible for any one of us to divorce himself from his status as a member and to occupy a seat in the galleries of the house and listen to this debate, what would have been the main impression made upon his mind? As I pondered that thought during the last few days I could not help feeling that perhaps the first and most definite impression an impartial outsider would receive would be the conviction that there was a singular indifference in this house to the problem of unemployment. a problem which agitates the mind of the public from one end of Canada to the other, and which in thousands of households is looked upon as little less than a tragedy. Yet day after day and hour after hour it appeared to me that there was an attitude of indifference and apathy towards a problem so serious that it might reasonably be expected that we would forget differences of opinion and endeavour to mobilize our abilities and our thoughts towards solving it.
The second thought that would come to me were I in that position of impartiality would be this. The numerous useful suggestions made by members on all sides of the house-a great many of them from the Liberal benches as well as from over here-were received often in a spirit of hostility. There was resistance to them; there was a tendency to resent suggestions that obviously were good, sound and useful. That is the second impression that has been made upon my mind.
The third is this. Can it be possible that we in this parliament-and for the moment I include all of us-are really unaware of the vital and tragic problem of unemployment that exists in Canada to-day? Is it possible that parliament is the only place in Canada where there is unawareness of its existence? Yet to me, from the general attitude and atmosphere up to this moment, this seems to be not an unfair judgment of the house as it is.
Sir Robert Peel almost a hundred years ago, under conditions not dissimilar to those now prevailing in Canada, when it will be recalled that prior to the repeal of the corn laws there was great destitution in the old land, in presenting his budget to parliament, stated at the very outset-the words I have not under my
2946	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
hand, but I have them in my mind-that the most essential thing was to admit and recognize the problem; once that was done we could progress, said he, to the treatment of the problem or solution. That is one thing at least, it seems to me, upon which parliament could be united-that there is a definite, and not a temporary, condition of unemployment and suffering and insecurity and distress in this country. Having admitted that, having laid it down as the underlying condition with which we are seeking to deal, we should be able to approach the question in a sympathetic way.
We are all aware of the problem individually. I know it; and may I say to the minister that I was a little disturbed at the question he would repeatedly put to one member after another who was presenting his view of the problem: " What evidence has the member to support that statement?" Well, if in discussing this or similar problems in the house we are to ibe narrowed down to such utterances as we are in a position to substantiate in a court of law, there is no hope for free discussion in parliament. I stand here and say on my responsibility as a member of parliament that I know this problem exists. We all know it. I know it because like many other members-I am no exception in this respect-I have touched it personally, yes, and indirectly by visiting camps and talking with men by the score, by the hundreds. We all know the problem exists; there is no question about that.
Now I look at the terms of the resolution. Frankly I had hoped at the opening of the session of 1939 some clear and definite policy would be announced to deal with unemployment. But the resolution is, I believe, the same as last year, if not the same as four sessions ago. Let me just call the attention of the house to its terms:
That it is expedient-
I pause at the word " expedient." It is not a question of expediency; it is a question of vital necessity. But I pass over that.
That it is expedient to bring in a measure-
What for?
-to provide assistance in the alleviation of unemployment.
In other words, we stop right there and simply say in plain, simple language that we have before us still a temporary problem which is bothering the country and we propose to alleviate it. We propose to carry on with the same measures we have had over the years in the past, which will get us away from the problem for the moment. The resolution goes on to say, referring to agricultural distress:
TMr. Stevens.]
-and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the general interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament.
This is the next important part of the resolution, and it is exactly what we have had in several sessions gone by:
-also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
There is nothing in that whole resolution to inspire any hope that we as a parliament are going to give serious consideration to this problem.
Let me proceed to the government's position as it is reflected in certain utterances of the minister and of members supporting the government. I cite these utterances not in a spirit of criticism, although I shall perhaps criticize them in a certain sense, but rather for the purpose of summing up the government's approach to this question.
One utterance which was made and repeated on several occasions was, "The poor ye have always with you." I repeat that not merely for the sake of reiteration, but for the purpose of suggesting that the citation of those sacred words in connection with parliament's attitude towards unemployment is a tragic travesty of this sublime utterance. The repetition in these circumstances of those words showed a total lack of appreciation of what they really mean. I think we might remember another utterance, "Bear ye one another's burdens," as being infinitely more appropriate at the present time than to taunt the unemployed with the fact that "unfortunately w'e have always had with us people such as you." Is it any solace or encouragement to the thousands of young and older men and women who are in this predicament simply to say to them: The poor we have always with us? The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) may have reflected the view of a great many hon. members when he uttered those words and related them to unemployment. These are his words:
It is an old disease of the human race. Jesus mentioned it when he said, "The poor ye have always with you." It was recorded in the days of the Roman empire, and it came to Spain during the collapse which followed the expansion after the discovery of the continent of North America. It was present in England after the battle of Waterloo. ... It followed the Crimean war, the United States civil war, and the great war.
I will finish the quotation in a moment, but I pause to suggest to my hon. friend, and to others who applauded him so vigorously, that merely to say that time after time

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
throughout history there has been distress is no discharge of our present responsibility as leaders of the state.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I did not say so.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am aware that any great disturbance such as the last war will inevitably bring results injurious to the human race. One cannot escape them. But, with all the experience of the past available to us, and with all the modern facilities we possess to deal with these conditions, we should be applying our best knowledge and efforts and taking advantage of all our accumulated science and skill to overcome, or at any rate to lessen, suffering, even though, as my hon. friend has shown, the cause and the effect may have historic precedent.
It is a singular fact that the hon. member for Huron North put his finger upon the only thing on which the government depends to cure unemployment; because only yesterday the minister made this statement:
As one looks ahead, one cannot but feel that our ability as a country to absorb our unemployed in industry depends in a very large measure, if not entirely, upon a resumption of normal conditions of international trade.
I am not ridiculing this statement, not for a moment, but I am pointing out that it
represents the policy of the government. The minister made a similar statement four sessions ago, in 1936. He made it last year. I do not recall whether it was made in 1937, but I assume it was. He has made it on numerous occasions on the public platform. In that declaration he reflects the viewpoint of the government, because the leader of the government has frequently expressed a similar view. We must therefore accept it as the government's policy for the correction of the condition of unemployment in Canada. I for one do not admit that it is an adequate answer to the problem, and I will tell the minister and the house why.
In the first place, we do not control world trade. The measure of our influence over the movement of trade to-day is probably less than it was fifty years ago, although since that time the expansion of our commerce has been considerable. The simple reason is, as I have repeatedly stated in this chamber, that country after country, until virtually all of them can be included, has adopted a definite and fixed policy of internal control of external trade. Quotas, high tariffs, prohibitions of one kind and another, have been imposed. To-day it is not at all a question of free trade versus protection-that issue is outmoded; today it is a question of quotas. There is scarcely a country which is not dealing with external trade through bilateral agreements and quotas; and for us to stand back and say that we are going to wait patiently and supinely until by some miracle the convictions and prejudices of other countries are removed, until in some mysterious way trade starts once again to move to our advantage, is not only a sorry position for parliament to take, but incidentally, is a tragic answer to the unemployed!
The minister yesterday-again I am not criticizing him; I cite it for the purpose of reviewing the situation as I see it to-day- was asked. "What is the cause?" I think the hon. member who asked the question ought to have paused and realized that almost any simple person can ask a question, but sometimes it is exceedingly difficult to answer.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It is a large order.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It does not display any great degree of perspicacity to ask a question of that kind. The minister, of course, was embarrassed in his answer. But he did say, and I would not for a moment disagree, that there is no one single cause of unemployment; it is due to a variety of causes. He, trained economist that he is, knows that is true. But why does he stick to this mythical remedy, namely, the possible expansion of external
2948	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
trade, as the only cure? He admits that there is no single cause of unemployment; certainly the fall in external trade was not the only cause. That is certain; he knows it better than I do. He knows that one cause which perhaps has had a larger measure of effect than others is the scientific development of machinery, the mechanization of industrial plants. This is not a temporary condition; it is permanent, it is definite. It is there, and we have to face it.
In justice to myself let me say-not vaingloriously at all, but merely by way of emphasizing my sincerity-that a socialist rose at one of my meetings in the election of 1930 and asked me this question: "Mr. Stevens, if you are elected, will you declare that your party can cure unemployment?" I said, "No; I will make no such declaration. And I will tell you why. Because," I said, "this condition of unemployment is in substantial measure due to new and scientific methods in industry and the expansion and use of machinery, and it would probably take us a considerable time to understand it and to absorb those thrown out of employment by the machine." I remember using this illustration, which at the time was a sound one, and to-day is even more to the point than it was then. I cited the electric light bulb. I said that up until 1923-I think that was the year-it took one operative all day to make 40 electric light bulbs. Then a machine was perfected which would make some 70,000 to 80,000 of them in an hour. I believe that since then the number has gone up to something like 250,000. I pointed out that that machine actually displaced 900 operatives. In reply to the question put at that time I said that a major cause of unemployment was the introduction of just such machines as that.
I know the minister agrees with me when I say that these and other factors intimated by him yesterday are the causes of the present distressed industrial condition. Why, then, do the minister and the government cling to this mythical thing, expansion of trade, as the only solution for unemployment? For that is the only policy they have, other than, as this resolution says, to alleviate it through loans to the provinces. We know that there are many causes of unemployment; but my point is that many things will have to be done by this government, by industry, by finance, by provincial governments, by municipalities, yes, by individuals, by service clubs such as waited on my hon. friend the other day-many things will have to be done by all these agencies before the problem is solved. But it is the duty of the federal government to mobilize these forces and to see that we

get out of this great economic and social machine which we call Canada the maximum results in efficiency. We have a magnificent economic machine; we have financial organizations capable of handling all the credit that is available and properly disposing of it-there is no need for any new machinery in that regard. We have an industrial machine that is equal to those of the leading countries of the world, if not in some respects, as I am told, ahead of many. It may be said that these are platitudes, but sometimes one has to indulge in platitudes in order that we may bring ourselves down to earth. We have all these things; yet there is something radically wrong. Last year the minister recognized the point I am now making; he said one thing that was necessary was to have private interests function properly. Well, he is no nearer now to getting private interests functioning than he was then.
Can one offer condemnation of a condition without being thought guilty of disrespect to the minister or to members of the government? I should like to say to him and to the Prime Minister and to his colleagues that I do not know one of them whom individually I do not respect and honour. But I must say without reserve that in this regard they have shown appalling ineptitude and incapacity.
I know someone will be tempted to say to me, "Oh, but what happened before 1935?" Are we going to waste our time in recriminations-what happened in 1935-what happened in 1930? Let me say that I have no patience with it; let the dead past bury its dead. What I am concerned about is what we are doing in 1939.
Let me call the minister's attention to the record as it is. In 1936 he came into this house a bright, cultured, trained young mind. This country said at the time, and I was one who said it, that in this Minister of Labour we have a young man who is mentally equipped to cope with this great task. I take second place to none in my appreciation of the complexity and tremendous scope of the task. But he came here with that blessing on his shoulders from the countiy. In the first session he showed a grasp of economic problems probably superior to that of almost any other member who spoke in the house at that time. He showed an understanding of the subject, the technique of it was familiar to him, the phraseology, the nomenclature of economics was at his command. He said to us, "Now, I want you to be patient, because we are going to appoint a royal commission-" this was in 1936-"and when that commission reports, when I as a trained economist have before me the assembly of all the facts, then

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
look out-we will do something." A year went by. In 1937 he told us to be patient, the commission was still sitting, there was no report yet. Well, while I cannot claim experience in economics, I can claim some experience in parliamentary practice, and the minister will recall that in 1936 I told him from my seat in the house that that commission would not report for two years. I was laughed at.
So in 1937 we were asked to be patient. The house was patient, the unemployed were patient. Then came 1938, and lo and behold we had the report 1 Here was an achievement. The young minister came before the house and tabled the report. True, his neighbour threw the report on the floor and ridiculed it, but I did not. I read it, and I recognized in it certain merits-not quite as high a degree of merit as was assigned to it by my hon. friend a moment ago; but the report did focus attention on the factors entering into the unemployment problem. I think most of us who have studied the question were fairly well acquainted with them before, but we did not have them presented in the clever, orderly precise manner in which they are set out in this report. From that standpoint we had a good report, an excellent report, in which a number of very useful suggestions were made.
In 1938 the minister came before the house and said, "Look, I have the report; now watch me." Well, a year has gone by. I am not going to be so prejudiced, shall I say, as to suggest to the minister to-day that conditions are worse than they were a year ago. We all know that. I am not going to say they are worse to-day because the minister has taken no action, because I know in my heart that there are factors that enter into the matter, factors in commerce and industry that influence the up and down movement of trade. But it would be just as fair and truthful for me to say that as it is to cite figures for 1933 and then figures for 1938. 1937 or 1936. These comparisons are worthless. I say to the minister very frankly that there has been a general world depression, or as they call it this time a recession, since a year ago; there is no question about that. But that does not exculpate the minister in respect of the grave duty of implementing the report, which has not been done in any measurable degree.
I am not going into details in regard to aspects of the question that have been analysed here over and over again, but I want to say this, and I will make my statement so broad that there will be no need of details. The minister now claims that instead of the $30,000,000 or whatever it was we voted for
this housing scheme being all government money, as we understood, that total was to be made up of both government and private money. But where we voted $30,000,000 for that purpose we should have voted $100,000,000. Where we voted $40,000,000 for another kind of activity we should have voted $100,000,000. Oh, yes; someone will say, "Where is the money to come from?" That question was asked in 1931, when I made a similar proposal. All we have to do is to pause and consider this fact, that since and including 1931 this country, dominion, provincial and municipal, has raised and expended over $900,000,000 on direct relief. It is an appalling sum. In 1931 I suggested $100,000,000 for housing. I suggested it again a couple of years ago, and I suggest it again now. When I am asked, "Can you raise it?" my answer is that of course we can raise it. We have raised money to the extent of $900,000,000, and wasted it. It has gone down the sewer and we have nothing to show for it except wrecked lives and young people whose lives have been sapped of ambition.
I would ask the Minister of Labour, the Prime Minister and the government to forget every speech made by members of the opposition and take only the speeches made by their own followers, depicting conditions in their own ridings. These were what might be called favourable critics. Read those speeches; remember the expenditure by this country of $900,000,000-Tory government and Grit government, if you like

and think of what we have to-day. It is an appalling situation. Then I am asked how we would raise $100,000,000 for this or that. It can be done.
In this report the minister is told by the commission, and truthfully, that one of the reasons building construction has not gone ahead in municipalities in Canada is that there is such a weight of local taxation. Two years ago, in this house, I think, I suggested that as a federal parliament-and I am prepared to explain this in detail-under agreement we might subsidize the cities and municipalities of Canada to the extent of twenty-five per cent of their taxation, provided they would immediately lower their taxes by twenty-five per cent and hold them at that level for a period of years. If you did that you would provide an impetus to building construction. These are not questions which you can blueprint and say you know all about their beginning and end; they are questions to be attacked day by day and hour by hour. As I said in regard to another matter a few weeks ago, they are administrative rather than legislative questions. It is not more legislation we want; it is administration, the will to do, the
2950	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
conviction that something must be done, then getting at it and doing it. I repeat that there is no doubt whatever that it is within the power of this government to mobilize the forces of industry and finance so that this question can be solved, perhaps not to-morrow and not during the next year. But we have been going on now for nine years. Let no one say, "Well, five years of that was under the previous government." Of course it was, and I am not excusing that government. I am saying that we are here as a parliament. Let us divorce ourselves from one side or the other. We as a parliament have been sitting here for nine years, facing this problem, and we are no nearer a solution of its essential features to-day than we were nine years ago.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend interjects a question which illustrates the tragedy of this whole thing. Why, Mr. Chairman, I do not care what the United States has done; I am talking about Canada. I am talking about a young country, virile, full of power, energy and resource, with only eleven million people. If we cannot solve our own problems there is something wrong with us. The attitude of mind indicated in that question is what I have noted in this debate-always an effort to excuse oneself in thinking of the question. No one can entertain an idea or concept of the sort indicated by my hon. friend's query and at the same time have an earnest desire for the. solution of this question. It cannot be done; it is a mental impossibility.
I have no desire to detain the committee at great length, Mr. Chairman, but I feel extremely earnest albout this. I know many hon. members of this house have boys of their own, as I have. I know from my own boy and from his chums and friends that they are puzzled and worried. They do not know what they are to do. I know from my young married daughters and others that scores of their friends, perhaps comfortably cared for, do not know how they are going to arrange their social and economic affairs in order that they may start married life together. That is one of the underlying problems. Then I am visited, as all hon. members are, by scores of older men, forty and fifty and fifty-five and sixty years of age, who for these last few years have found themselves without the opportunity to work. I recall the tough times of the nineties. I went west early in the nineties, so when we talk about depressions I have been through them. But while perhaps there was more suffering from poverty in those days than there is to-day, yet there

were few cases where a man could not get enough work to enable him to eat. To-day that is not so.
When, the other day, I heard an hon. member refer to the unemployed without discrimination as derelicts and little better than criminals, I was shocked. I will give my estimate of the percentage represented by those who honestly want to secure work, and if the minister asks for evidence I will say the only evidence I have is my common sense and personal knowledge. I have talked to hundreds-I suppose thousands-in the last few years. I have gone up the lines and into their camps, shaken their hands and talked to them. I have talked to a lot of these fellows who came from my own province in the last two weeks. My own conviction is that about seventy-five per cent of those chaps are honest, earnest men, who want a job and nothing else. I am convinced of it. I will admit there are a certain number of slackers, derelicts, easy-going fellows among them, who do not want work. You always have that class. You will find them in the busiest of times.
I remember the boom period in Vancouver, back in 1908, 1909 and 1910 when conditions there were noted the world over for the rapidity with which money could be made. Yet even in those days, when I was a member of the city council, we had to keep certain families because of the indigent character of the head of the house. You always have that. But of these young men and of these older men I venture to say we can set it down as a fact that seventy-five per cent of them want one thing-an opportunity to work. And it will not do to say that if they had the enterprise their forefathers had, they would have work.
I can go back to my young days, a generation ago-

I am not saying the state owes every man a living, but I do

say this: The state owes it to society that where circumstances arise which prevent a man from getting an opportunity to work, the state must take cognizance of them and do what it can to remove them. And they can be removed, provided we realize what the minister said yesterday-that there is no single cause for unemployment, that there is no single remedy. But an application of numerous remedies through administrative effort would bring about a return to normal conditions.

speechtext:
Naturally I have no desire to delay the passage of my own resolution. At the same time I should like to comment briefly on a number of statements made by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens).
In the first place I wish to express appreciation of the manner in which he has spoken. I believe he honestly desired to give the fruits of his own thought on this very serious problem of unemployment, a problem which has been troubling us not for five years but, as the hon. member well knows, for a period of ten years, and not this country alone but, one might say, the entire world.
He chose as the text for his remarks a statement I made yesterday in response to a question from one of the members of the Social Credit party. The question, put suddenly to me, was in these terms: Do you believe it is possible for this country to absorb the unemployed? My answer to that question, given upon the basis of my own experience, was that with a return of normal conditions of international trade a great exporting country like Canada might expect to absorb its annual accretion of potential wage earners.
My hon. friend has suggested I put that forward as the only solution of the unemployment problem. I have no hesitation in saying I did put it forward as the most reasonable expectation confronting this exporting country for an absorption of its unemployed in private industry. When I made that statement I was only repeating what was said a few months ago by Oliver Stanley, president of the board of trade in England. I was only repeating, in different words, what has been said on more than one occasion by the Secretary of State for the United States. In these last years Mr. Cordell Hull has by his own efforts sought to negotiate bilateral trade treaties with as many countries as possible because of his conviction that in that way lay the most reasonable prospect of reviving trade, industry and employment in his own country.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

And so far he has utterly
failed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Well, I would not acknowledge that at' this time. I think even my hon. friend would agree that in these years there has been an extraordinary situation of international tension, of fear and of lack of confidence on the part of those who control the investment of private funds. Under these conditions even the best of trade treaties have not been able to produce their maximum effectiveness in respect of the trade of this or any other country.

Not more than fifteen per
cent.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me to go farther? In these last few years we have had a persistent condition of drought in western Canada. In other words we have not produced what normally would have been produced in that area and sold in foreign markets, such sales establishing purchasing power which would have assisted eastern industry.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

anyway?

There is no question, my
hon. friend will agree, that a very large proportion of our wheat is exported, and must depend upon export markets. But a very considerable section of our secondary industry-

-in this country also

If my hon. friend will

condition of drought you had an equally serious condition, namely that we were unable in Canada to produce wheat which could be sold, and that this wheat was simply held in our elevators; would he not acknowledge that such a situation would have as serious an effect upon industrial employment in eastern Canada? Most certainly it would.
The hon. member for Kootenay East suggested that there is no real solution for unemployment in the direction of international trade. But he, as a former minister of trade and commerce, would be the first to admit that for a country so constituted as Canada the maintenance of export markets is essential to the welfare of a very large and increasing section of not only our agricultural but our industrial life,

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That has never been in dispute.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: But my hon. friend does dispute-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I do not.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: -that there is a real hope of improving the employment situation through an improvement in international trade -because that is the statement I made, and the statement to which he has taken exception.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I know the minister does not wish to misrepresent what I have said.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Not at all; I do not for one moment say that international trade will not have a beneficial effect. It always has. We always welcome an expansion of international trade. But I say that to lean upon that-I will narrow it that much-to provide the major solution is, in my opinion, a dereliction of duty on our part. My point is that we must do much more than that.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will follow me, he agrees that we must produce more in this country in order to give greater employment. Is that correct? He has said we cannot

hope to produce more and find outlets in foreign markets for our production. How is he going to bring about the consumption of the more that he would produce in Canada in order to give greater employment?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: By giving more domestic employment.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: My hon. friend is simply following a vicious circle. I ask my hon. friend how he would answer that question.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I can answer it quite easily, but I certainly cannot answer it with a yes or no.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am wondering if my hon. friend is not really in the same position in his thinking as the members of the Social Credit group.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: If you cannot produce more [DOT] and have that production taken up in foreign markets, then obviously you must produce more and consume it within this country. How do you propose to do that?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I shall gladly answer that. Probably I will get a chance to deal with this before the committee rises. For the moment, my answer is that if we spent as much energy on practical measures which would assist in the solution of this question, dozens of which have been suggested, as we do in academic reasoning and regimentation backward and forward, we would make more progress.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I have long since passed the time when I was worried about that word "academic." I think it was the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) who applied it to me first, although later on he decided that "metaphysical" was a better word. Nevertheless, I prefer to go ahead with the argument, regardless of whether or not my hon. friend considers it to be academic. In my opinion it is practical common sense.
In answer to the question put to me yesterday I said that if we as a country lost our export markets, which would be a calamity the like of which we have never known before, we would find it more and more difficult to resist the pressure toward a self-contained economy. Perhaps that is what my hon. friend has in view. If we had a self-contained economy in this country, it could only be at a sacrifice of the standard of living of the people of this country, and also at a sacrifice of human liberties.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: To what standard of living is the minister referring?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The standard of living of a large section of our population, and not only

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
in western Canada. My hon. friend does not find it possible to follow me, but surely he knows as well as I that a. large section of the industrial structure of this country was not only built up but was maintained by the western market, which in itself has depended upon the markets of the world.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The markets of the world for wheat, which is the chief product of the west, have almost completely disappeared, that is, markets at reasonable prices. Furthermore, I have had enough experience in other countries of America to know that any country which depends chiefly upon its export trade of primary products for its standard of living has a standard of living so far below the lowest standard of living prevalent in this country, that God forbid that this country could ever be reduced that far. If this government would give reasonable encouragement to domestic industry, within eighteen months there would be an increase of thirty per cent in the number employed in the industrial life of this country. But that will not be achieved by devoting your entire attention to foreign markets for wheat which do not now exist and which are not soon likely to exist except in case of war.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The views which my hon. friend expresses now were expressed by him and his leader of that day before 1930. He and his government had every opportunity to put those views into effect. They did so with the emergency tariff of 1930, which produced the opposite result to that which he now says would follow.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Let me say in reply to the hon. gentleman that they produced this result-

speechtext: I should like to say to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that if at any time he wishes to interrupt me, it is all right for him to do so.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I was going to reply in only one sentence. My firm conviction is that the remedial tariff measures which the former Conservative government introduced in 1930, 1931 and 1932 saved this country from an almost complete disaster, and preserved in this country a standard of living, the like of which was to be found in but very few other countries. I know of none in which the standard of living is as high as that which was preserved in this country for our own people. It is true that in the later development of that policy certain measures which had been introduced were declared to be beyond the jurisdiction of this parliament, and therefore they failed. But some means must be found, either by further decisions of the courts or by agreement with the provincial authorities, whereby the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament may be so extended as to place in this parliament, not only the duty and responsibility but also the legislative authority necessary to enable us to enter upon a thorough solution of our social problems.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: We on this side acknowledge the value of the home market, but we have gone further than my hon. friend in that we have also recognized that in a country situated as Canada is, the home market is inextricably bound up with the maintenance of international markets. You cannot speak of a home market in a geographical sense: you can speak of it only in the sense that there lies within that market the purchasing power which can be used for the exchange of products. My hon. friend is perfectly well aware that in a great agricultural country like Canada you have to depend upon foreign markets in order to place that store of purchasing power in the pockets of our farm population.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: For about fifteen per cent of it, that is all.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
My hon. friend and those who sat with him adopted what I can only describe as a defeatist attitude toward international trade from 1930 to 1935. It was commonly said that apart from the British commonwealth of nations and the Ottawa agreements it was hopeless for this country to expect that it could recapture markets or establish markets that had never existed before. That was the whole trend of economic policy in this country from 1930 to 1935. But the Liberal party took the position, and takes the position now, that regardless of that trend, foreign markets have not been lost beyond recovery. And we practised that philosophy when we came into power. We gained a market which governments of Can-
2954	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
ada have been seeking to gain from confederation to the present day. We gained it first in 1935 and broadened it this year.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Where are they?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I refer to the market of the United States and the reciprocal trade agreement. I cannot believe, and I doubt if my hon. friend will believe, that a kind of economic policy established in certain countries of the world to-day which regards the importation of foreign products as a confession of economic failure is a policy that can continue to exist. We can, if we desire, produce oranges under glass in Canada, and provide employment in setting up greenhouses.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That is academic enough.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
That is simply the policy I have just referred to, carried to what I admit is an absurd conclusion; but it is the policy itself that is absurd, and that is why the conclusion is absurd. You have in Germany to-day a country which is committed to an economic policy of producing synthetically products which formerly were imported on a basis of exchange with other countries. You have an economic policy in Germany and fascist countries which holds that all things needed by their populations must be produced within those countries. I cannot believe that a policy of that kind, founded as it is on an eternal fallacy, can survive. But just now we are passing through that particular phase of economic philosophy. No government true to its convictions can admit that such a policy can survive, and that is why we have held to the view that we are going to search for foreign markets regardless of the obstacles in our way. That is why we believe that in a country like Canada we must find foreign markets for our agricultural products, and for an increasing number of our industrial products, in order to stimulate industrial activity and expand employment.
One other word before I close. The hon. member for Kootenay East has referred to the recommendations of the national employment commission. I have no objection to discussing that subject, which was referred to yesterday by the leader of the opposition. The national employment commission made recommendations of several kinds. In the first place they made recommendations to deal with an immediate situation. The first problem they faced was that of single unemployed men, particularly in the prairie provinces, and they recommended the adoption of a farm employment plan. That recommendation was accepted immediately by the government and

put into effect, and under that plan we have had in the last three years an average of
40,000	men and women put into employment in the prairie provinces.
The national employment commission also took this position so far as stimulating internal industry was concerned, that the industry which offered the best prospect of stimulation, the building industry, might very well be encouraged under a plan called the home improvement plan. Again that recommendation was carried into effect.
Other recommendations of the commission touched upon public works which would contribute directly to employment. The commission took the view expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay East that there was no real solution for unemployment in public works. They recommended rather that the government should not, except at an acute period of depression, adopt any large program of public works. They realized that public works had their function in a depression period, that there can be legitimate expansion, but that such expansion should be directed rather to the type of project which had at the end of it increased employment in the country. Here again we followed the recommendations of the national employment commission in the actual projects undertaken. We have spent money on mining roads, tourist roads, national parks, historic sites, in directions where the expenditures have given definite stimulus to the tourist industry of Canada.
Now I come to other recommendations of the commission. The commission recognized two constitutional positions: the one an existing position, the other a possible position with respect to grants in aid to the provinces. Under the existing position the commission recommended that grants should be given with certain stipulations attached, designed to bring about a greater degree of efficiency in the distribution of relief. Those recommendations were substantially carried into effect and are continued in effect in the agreements we have with the provinces.
The other recommendations of the commission with respect to the ultimate assumption by the dominion government of the cost of relief given to employables were contingent upon the adoption of a national scheme of unemployment insurance, and if my hon. friend will read the report of the commission he will see that this is the only fair inference that can be drawn from it. I submitted to my hon. friend, if he shakes his head as an evidence of failure to accept that view-

speechtext:
As an evidence of hopelessness.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: -that he has not read the report in its entirety.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I have read it and reread it.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Then he has failed entirely to catch its meaning. In so far as that recommendation of the commission was concerned, it was based upon the adoption of a national scheme of unemployment insurance.
In so far as other recommendations of the commission are concerned, the recommendation with respect to youth training was carried into effect in the session of 1937-38 and has been continued ever since.
There was another recommendation with respect to the rehabilitation of older unemployed persons, but in order to carry that recommendation and other recommendations into effect it was necessary to get the full and cordial cooperation of provincial governments. I went with Mr. Purvis myself to certain provincial governments and discussed the rehabilitation of older unemployed persons. I remember particularly a conference on that question in Quebec. All the members of the commission realized that these rehabilitation plans could only be carried into effect on the basis of dominion-provincial cooperation. It so happened that the government of Quebec was unwilling to enter into those plans, preferring what they termed a policy of giving work to those in need through public works. The same was true of a number of the other provinces.
In so far as housing is concerned, I have already mentioned the home improvement plan. There was in addition the low rental housing plan. That too now forms a part of the National Housing Act. My hon. friend from Kootenay East suggests that only a very limited sum is available under our various pieces of housing legislation, and he would have 1100,000,000 made available; but if he will add up what has been done under the home improvement plan under part I of the National Housing Act, under part II of the National Housing Act, and under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, he will have a figure in excess of $100,000,000 made available for the purposes mentioned.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
All provided by this
government?

speechtext: By way of loan and guarantee.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No, that amount is made available by way of loan under the legislation indicated.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Would the minister give a simple illustration of what he means? Take,
for instance, the question of loans. Who advances the money, and what proportion is advanced by private interests?

speechtext: As my hon. friend is aware, different systems prevail under different acts. Under part I of the National Housing Act it is by way of guarantee to the private lending companies. subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: How much?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, that legislation does not come under the Department of Labour.

speechtext: Again, under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, a fixed amount is made available for purposes of loans to these various construction projects. I mention these matters because it is very easy for hon. members to rise in their places and say, this or that has not been done. I think that sometimes it would be useful if there were at least a recognition that these various measures have been undertaken, because as far as this government is concerned we are able to point to a record of definite policies which have been put into operation to meet this problem-not to cure it; no one for a moment would suggest that. But I say that, in addition to long-range measures designed to improve the trading position of this country and thereby its industrial activity, we have put into effect measures, some of them recommended by the national employment commission, some of them put into effect before the national employment commission began to function, which have had their effect in improving the situation in this country.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I will deal first with the latter question, as to the national employment commission's report. We have carried out, I suggest, the more important recommendations of that commission which were within our power to discharge.
