Unemployment and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Does the minister think the government has adequately discharged its responsibility? That is what I am asking.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: On that point, which is the other question put by my hon. friend, I as Minister of Labour would never be satisfied that we had done all that could be done while the situation remains as it is now. I hope there is more that we can do. We are doing something all the time. Only the other day an announcement was made with respect to forest conservation camps in this country. That work was not initiated for the first time this year; it was an expansion of what was done before in an experimental way. I am satisfied that we have done many things which have made a definite contribution to the employment of the unemployed, and we have at the same time avoided certain policies, some of them in existence under the preceding administration, which in the long run would have had an injurious effect upon the position of the unemployed. I believe that any government in power in any part of the world at this time is compelled to proceed by way of trial and error, and any government has to decide how much it is going to deal with this problem by way of creating an increased dependence upon governments, and how much it is going to depend upon the cooperation of private industry and the expectation that private industry under improving conditions of trade will be able to expand employment.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Would the minister
answer that simple question: Does he consider that the government's policy towards unemployment is an adequate discharge of its duty to the country in that respect?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: This government, from the time it has come into office, has addressed itself to the unemployment problem with deep conviction and, I suggest, with as great a desire to obtain results as any government could have. The results have not always been equal to our desires or our expectations, but I do not fear, regardless of the consequences, to go before the people of this country upon our record with respect to this matter.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am sure it must be gratifying to hon. members sitting in this section of the chamber to have listened to the argument between the two old-line parties as to which has done the most towards solving the problem of unemployment. One hon. member says, which has done the least; I think it amounts to the same thing.

I listened carefully to this debate, especially while the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) was ridiculing the Liberals and while the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) was ridiculing the Conservatives. In one of his remarks the hon. member for Kootenay East blamed machines for a great deal of the present unemployment. He pointed out that through the advance of science and invention, machines have materially displaced labour. That statement is quite in accord, I believe, with modern data. He went on to point out how greatly thereby unemployment had increased, and right there is where he fell down; for he had no suggestion as to how we should take care of the people who have been displaced by machinery. That is the difficulty experienced by both the old-line parties; they come right up to the problem, but they do not go on to solve it. I was listening with interest to the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay East, to find what he would do with these men who have been displaced by the machine, but I am still at a loss to know what is his solution. He stressed the point that we should not look to what happened before 1933; that we should not examine the past record of the Conservative party, or what had been done or left undone in the past by the Liberal party, but that we should start in on a new plan. But it seems to me that in all fairness, since the two old-line parties are following exactly the same policy they pursued in the past, it would be of great benefit to this country if we investigated rather carefully the results of their policies; for I believe we would find that in consequence of those policies Canada is in a worse position than it ever was in before. A figure of something like 400,000 has been mentioned as the number now unemployed. That in itself shows what the country can look forward to if we continue with the policies which are advocated by either of the old-line parties.
It is easy for the Conservative party as represented by the hon. member for Kootenay East to say to the government, "You should go out and do this; you should inaugurate a scheme of public works or some other plan." The hon. member went on to say that he would raise a hundred million dollars for this purpose, but when he was asked where he would get the money he threw up his hands and said, "Let us not bother about that." The Minister of Labour on the other hand pointed out that his party had spent more than that amount, and the way they got the money was by borrowing or by taxation, but largely in the form of loans. It is through just such action as that that the dominion has gone into debt over three and a half billions of

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
dollars, and that last year we paid out in interest roughly $137,000,000; or, putting it in another way, we paid out in interest charges on borrowed money over thirty cents of every dollar obtained through taxation. That is one of the reasons why we are so heavily in debt to-day, and one of the reasons, indirectly, why there is so much trouble in the land. Better evidence of this could not be put before the people of Canada than we have heard in the last half hour in the arguments between representatives of the Conservative party and the Liberal party.
I think any fair-minded citizen must come to the conclusion that the policy of either of those parties, policies which have been tried off and on for a hundred years, or at least since the time of confederation, are certainly no solution for the difficulties that we face to-day. I was interested when the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) was referring to the eleven-point program presented by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). At one moment he said it was a commendable program and in the next breath he condemned it, saying that public works are no solution. So the old-line parties argue back and forth; one sets up a snow man and the other knocks it down and they get nowhere.
I did not intend to take up much time in this debate, believing that the house wanted, as was indicated to me this afternoon, to get along with the business of the session; but when I find the time of the house being wasted so uselessly as it has been in some of the lengthy addresses and discussions that have been going on, and especially when some hon. members on the other side refer to our young unemployed people in such scurrilous language as was used the other day, I think it behooves me to say a few words on their behalf.
In my constituency I have two cities that are as industrial as any part of the west, the city of Drumheller, which is entirely industrial, and the industrial section of Calgary. I resent strongly any hon. member from his place in this house trying to convey the impression abroad that these unemployed young people are worthless dubs and spineless vagabonds and so on. I have seen men of the unemployed ranks in Drumheller and have spoken to their organization, and I defy anyone in this house or anywhere else to find a more orderly or more intelligent group of people. I often wonder what would be the effect upon these young people, who, after all, are the flower of the land, should some of them be sitting in the galleries of this house and hearing the remarks which were made here by one or two
hon. members on the other side and which were so loudly applauded by other hon. members on the other side-

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That is not true; all government members did not applaud.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I just wonder what effect it would have on them, thinking: There is the man I helped to elect; there are the people who are supposed to be here solving our economic problems, yet the only thing offered as a solution is to refer to the unemployed in such unscrupulous language as was used the other day.
I am gratified to have the Minister of Labour acknowledge that the Liberal party have no solution for unemployment.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They did not acknowledge that.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: And I am also gratified to know that the Conservative party have acknowledged the same thing.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What has the hon. member's party done?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yet they go on fooling the people, hoping by that means to get into power in another election.
The other day I took up a report in regard to relief camps, an interim report made by a committee set up by the Minister of Labour to investigate these conditions. The committee consisted of R. A. Rigg, director of the employment service branch of the Department of Labour, Humphrey Mitchell, formerly member of parliament for Hamilton East, and E. W. Bradwin, Ph.D., of Toronto, principal of the Frontier college. In the re< port it is said:
With the official release of the report, the Hon. Norman McL. Rogers, Minister of Labour, issued a prefatory statement as follows:-
"The members of the committee were selected for the task because of their special knowledge in regard to the several aspects of the relief camp problem."
So the minister did not pick them indiscriminately; he used great care in picking these men. The statement continues:
"They approached their investigation with a sympathetic understanding of the human factors in the problem and with a knowledge as well of the practical considerations which must also have their bearing on government policy. This report is being released because of the widespread interest in relief camps throughout the country. We propose to take the people into our confidence in regard to the whole matter. Wherever it is possible to do so, I think it is desirable to throw a clear light on a problem in order that the taxpayers and citizens generally may know the reason for the adoption of particular policies."
2958	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
This interim report was made to the minister on January 31, 1936. I do not intend to read the full report, but the minister said the other day that the only policy that the Liberal party had for the alleviation of the condition of the unemployed was the hope that the agricultural industry would absorb them. This was a select committee, carefully chosen to report on these conditions. Let me read some of their recommendations:
We beg to report specifically on the five phases of our inquiry, set forth in the minister's letter of reference, as follows:-
1. The evidence we have accumulated compels us to advise that continuance of the camps for a temporary period is necessary.
This is the part I should like hon. members to notice:
The facilities for employment in private industry and agriculture are insufficient to absorb any considerable number of those in the camps at the present time.
There was a committee, carefully selected by the minister for their special ability to deal with this question, and they clearly state that unemployment could never be taken care of through the absorption of the unemployed in agriculture or private industry. Yet the minister rises in his place in this house now and says the only possible chance that these unemployed have is that agriculture will absorb them. That is in direct contradiction to the recommendations made by his so-carefully-picked committee.
The report continues:
Relief camp workers may be classified under four broad types.
I refer to this particular section in order to show that the people in these relief camps are not such as they were branded by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) and the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren). The report says:
There is a goodly percentage of young men who still retain an eager desire to occupy a useful place in society and to devote their energies and abilities to industrial, commercial or agricultural employment.
The majority of the relief camp workers consists of that body of men of more mature age, who, while not so keenly ambitious as the younger element, are, nevertheless, yearning for the opportunity to maintain themselves independently through the medium of normal, remunerative, private or public employment.
Anyone who has had to do with the unemployed knows that by far the greater percentage of them is of that very description. And here is this selected committee appointed to investigate this subject coming out with exactly the same words, that they are only too willing to take employment, provided

they get a decent wage, but when they are offered twenty cents a day I do not blame them for not working, I would not myself.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member's group does work.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
That may be applicable to some hon. members. It does not destroy the truth of what I said. The report continues:
There is a group of young men whose ages range from eighteen to twenty-five years-
This paragraph perhaps pertains more closely to those who do not act quite in accordance with our views, some of those young people in the camps who possibly become leaders of so-called insurrection movements in these camps. It says:
There is a group of young men whose ages range from eighteen to twenty-five years, many of whom have never had other than occasional casual employment and who, therefore, have not acquired the habit of working or the sense of individual responsibility to society. These young fellows have suffered through thwarted ambitions and the lack of visible grounds of hope for the future, and have become an easy prey to the subversive influences of communistic or anarchistic philosophy, sedulously propagated by experienced agitators. Most of these young men are gifted with average intelligence and if they had grown up surrounded by the influences of a normal environment, which included useful work, they would no doubt have given a good account of themselves. Under the influences among which they have lived during the past few years, however, they constitute a real menace to the maintenance of our existing institutions.
While some of the young fellows in these camps may not be up to the one hundred per cent standard, after all they are not the ones to blame. We in this house, by the legislation we pass, make it impossible for them to get out and get employment, and we are the ones to blame, as is so aptly pointed out in this report, which continues:
It is of the most pressing importance that very determined efforts should be made to explore the resources of Canada-
That is exactly in accordance with the opinions of this group. Time after time we have said that the full resources, natural and human, of this dominion, should be put to work to solve this question.
-both public and private, for the purpose of developing fields of industrial employment in order that the men included in the types A, B and C might be absorbed as speedily as possible in useful work at current rates of wages and thus become self-sustaining.
With this accurate information before him I am surprised that the minister would suggest that he hopes agriculture will be able to absorb the unemployed. He must know that this cannot be done.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
permit me, I was asked if I could give an example, and I mentioned agriculture.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
That is
correct; the minister did mention agriculture as the possible hope.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: As one possible hope.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Let us
consider the other industries, because the report I just read showed conclusively that neither private industry nor agriculture would ever be able to absorb any material number of these men. Even if you take both together you will not be able to absorb them. Last year I happened to visit one of the automobile factories of this country, which I think was working about six or seven months a year. In conversation with the manager I said, "Why don't you fellows work the full twelve months?" We were standing near a window; the manager pointed through that window and said, "If you will get rid of that line of trucks out there I will put twice as many in their place, and we will work twelve months a year to keep that yard filled if you can keep the trucks going out of the yard." I think he just about hit the nail on the head.
You cannot expect private industry to absorb these men. The Conservative party adheres to the old, outworn theory that if you stimulate industry that is all you have to do. That is far from the truth. It is not necessary to stimulate industry by parliamentary methods. If you will make it possible for industry to sell its products, industry will do its own stimulating. If you increase the purchasing power of the people so that they can buy the products of industry; you need not worry about industry being speeded up; it will take care of itself in that regard.
When we think of the few opportunities available to these unfortunate people, compared with what we used to have, the situation is tragic. Especially is that so when hon. members rise in this house and say these fellows can go out and get jobs if they want them. I recall the way in which I got money in the fall of the year, in my younger days, when I was going back to university. I came to the conclusion that all I had to do was go out and get a job in the harvest field, and that was exactly what I did. We were paid $11 a day for a man and team throwing bundles. You did not have to go out and look for a job; it was practically there at your door. Last year I met some young fellows from Ontario and Quebec out in western Canada during harvest time, and said to them, "Goodness gracious, why do you come away out here looking for jobs?" Their reply 71492-187
19, 1939	2959
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
was, "Well, we heard there was a chance of some work in the harvest fields out here." That was the condition fifteen or twenty years ago, but that time has gone. In the old days threshing machines required fifteen or sixteen teams with a crew of perhaps twenty or twenty-two men. Now the same size crop on the same amount of land is harvested by just the farmer and his son, working with a combine. Because of our improved methods of farming the day is past when agriculture can absorb any considerable number of the unemployed.
That is particularly so because of the way in which agriculture is being treated, or the way in which the Liberal party hope to treat it by the new legislation, under which they do not intend to pay the farmers more than thirty cents a bushel on the farm. I am sure that will not encourage farmers to hire more men and help reduce the number on the relief rolls. How can they do it? It is an utter impossibility for agriculture to absorb any number of unemployed when the farmer receives only thirty cents a bushel for wheat; the idea is preposterous.
I live in perhaps one of the richest provinces of Canada. In Alberta we have a tremendous amount of coal as well as an oil field which, I believe, is potentially one of the largest in the British empire. What is the dominion government doing to help those two great industries to absorb some of the unemployed? One would have thought, Mr. Chairman, that once the oil field of Alberta became a proven fact this government would have done everything possible to make it a going concern, instead of putting every possible obstacle in the way of the provincial government. Why, according to the newspapers, even Germany wanted to assist in the construction of a pipe line, and not long ago I read that members of the Alberta government had gone to England in order to obtain sufficient money to carry on the oil industry of that province. Surely it is a sorry outlook for this dominion when a province has to go entirely outside this country in order to obtain money to assist in the development of one of the greatest oil fields in the empire.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Did they get the money?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I do not know, but should it be necessary to go to England or to Germany to get it?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member should be able to answer that question.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is
exactly as the hon. member for Kootenay East said a short time ago; if we need this money

2960	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
we can get it, especially in connection with a matter of such importance as the Turner valley oil field, and particularly at a time like this when we are about to be thrown into war and when we shall need all the oil reserves we can possibly secure. Yet here is one of the greatest industries-and what are we doing? In the east the people buy gasoline from United States sources. We cannot get decent freight rates for the transport of Alberta oil to eastern Canada; that is our greatest difficulty. If members of the government would devise means of developing the coal fields and oil fields of Alberta, and a method whereby we could trade those commodities for the fish of Nova Scotia or the manufactured goods of eastern Canada, we would be getting down to rock-bottom, and the root of the whole question.
Yet, here we sit idly by, trying to follow the policies which have been followed for hundreds of years, at a time when this Dominion of Canada is faced with a debt of about seven and a half billion dollars. And the hon. member for Kootenay East says, "Well, go on and get more money." But he does not say where he will get it from. If we would centre our attention more particularly on the distribution of goods within our own country we would be getting closer to a solution of this problem. Hon. members may ask me: "How are you going to do it?" I don't care how you do it; I am not concerned in that-just so long as you do it.
A little while ago we were talking about export trade. The party to which I belong has nothing against export trade but I think our first requisite is that we take care of our home market. When we have completely satisfied that market we can ship our wheat, if you like, in exchange for something we do not have. H we have a wheat surplus, why not ship it to Germany and get their farm machinery in exchange? "Oh, but," some people say, "what about our industry in Canada?" All' right; arrange matters so that our machinery industry in Canada can trade machinery for wheat, and so that we may have an interchange of goods. When we talk about the unity of Canada we ought to remember that that is where it lies. And I say in all seriousness that unless we find some way of equally distributing those goods within Canada, and thereby bringing eastern and western Canada more closely together, the government are going to have more trouble on their hands than they have to-day through unemployment, because the whole nation will be unemployed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
What will you do with
the wheat that is not consumed in Canada?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
What
would you naturally do with it?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am asking you.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: You would ship it out, of course; you would exchange it for something else you could not grow. But why should you ship out wheat when you are not now consuming all that can be consumed in Canada? Tell me that. Why should you have unemployed, or people on relief who do not get enough bread? Why, in Germany and Austria they even give their people bread.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They may give them bread, but they do not give them enough.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That might be.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: We have the same condition in Canada. All people can get some bread, but the difficulty is that all people cannot get enough bread to satisfy their needs.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: But a goodly share do not get enough to maintain them in decent health. The question is whether or not they can get enough. The question is: Do they get enough to maintain decent health?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: That is not the point the hon. member was arguing. I was dealing with his earlier argument, not the one he is now making.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I was saying that we should never look for export business until we have completely satisfied the requirements of our own home market. And I do not think you will ever find a solution until you do that very thing. This is not merely a difficulty which lies in any one province.
A clipping I have before me from Labour, published in Washington, refers to the meeting of the Canadian federation of mayors. This issue, of April 18, 1939, contains the following:
The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities is demanding a sweeping change in relief costs so as to relieve municipalities of their present share of responsibility.
This week the federation announced that everything indicated the relief problem will continue indefinitely, because there is no appreciable abatement in unemployment.
That was the statement made by the mayors from the different towns and cities in Canada, men who are conversant with conditions in their local municipalities. Surely they should know something of what they are talking about. The article goes on:
"Unemployment in our time," the federation holds, "is primarily a by-product of the economic state of the nation and, as such, is rightly a national responsibility."

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
I think that is true; it is a national responsibility.
What are we doing down here? It can be justly said that we are doing nothing. When one realizes that one province in the dominion made the promise to the federal government, " If you will keep your hands off us we will take care of our own difficulties and our own troubles, and we will not ask you for a nickel," he would think the dominion government would have been so tickled it would have been overjoyed to find out that that province was willing to go ahead on its own initiative. In 1935 the Prime Minister said he would keep his hands off. But certainly such was not the case.
The other day I ran across an article published on November 25, 1938, in which the question of unemployment is discussed. Allow me to assure hon. members that this did not appear in a social credit paper; on the contrary it appears in the Calgary Albertan, and is as follows:
The stark, naked fact of continued unemployment is ever before us. Worse still, it is now apparent that there is no orthodox cure for such a condition. War preparations have played their part in creating employment but it can only last as long as the war spirit is in the air. People are asking, "What will be our lot when building of armaments cease?"
And I just wonder: What will be our lot?
The national consciousness is perhaps slow to move to a new base, but we now have evidence that the continued cry of the new deal, technocracy, social credit and the many additional cries of others are having their effects. We are now moving, slowly perhaps, but surely, to a new concept of life and the whole structure of democracy is due for great changes within the next ten years.
In the end we must conform to physical facts. We may dodge them for a time but the day of reckoning comes. Governments everywhere are facing difficulties created by these bothersome facts. And we make bold to say that those who are opposed to change had better leave political pursuits severely alone.
There are two outstanding facts which claim the attention of our legislators to-day. The first is the great volume of debt being carried by governments, which is continually increasing, and the other is that the day has come when the home market is of more importance than any other. In those two facts we see the politics of to-morrow.
The scaling down of debts, and their repayment is coming to be regarded as a matter which gives great concern. For the cutting off of debt structure is bound to have its effect on the investment field. It will at once be seen that investment must find its field in industry instead of in debt-building and that again will increase the volume of employment if-the market can buy what is produced.
Around this latter point the controversies of to-morrow will rage. Consumer finance is the key to prosperity. The forgotten man must come into his own.
7 492-187J
May I endorse that statement. Until we have come to realize that we must finance consumption, never will we have solved unemployment, or any other question in the dominion.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
This is the first time I have taken part in this debate. I believe, however, that I have some right to speak, because had it not been for the relief camps and unemployment in my constituency my name would never have gone before it for nomination. I would remind the hon. member who has just spoken, an hon. member who is a student, one for whom I have profound respect and who has said that the two old parties are the same, that there is a universal law which states that there is change everywhere and no two things are ever alike. A little girl once asked her mother if, when she got married, she would have to live with the same man for twenty-five years. The mother replied, "Your dad is not the same man he was when I married him twenty-five years ago."
My experience is that there are at least three types of single unemployed. First, tl ire are the travellers, who were formerly known as the hoboes. The men of this type belong to the lowest classes. I believe their character is less dependable than that of the other two types to which I shall refer. We permitted a large number of these hoboes to sleep in our church basement in Fort William -during the week days of course-and at the end of the season they carried away the rugs which had been given to them to sleep upon and many other articles. When that happened I was just as much disappointed as was the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) when he had his bam burned and his horses and cattle destroyed. He said a few bad words, and I am not going to blame him very much for that.
I believe that among the men who hit the trail there are many who would prove capable if they could only get settled. The members of this house should take a personal interest in these men. We should not be afraid to go all the way with them, as the hon. member for Yukon (Mrs. Black) has suggested. There is another type of single unemployed, the city youth. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has said that not more than ten per cent of this class are unwilling to work. I do not know whether that is right because I have no data to prove it, but I should like to give the committee an example. I know one young man who graduated from our collegiate. I was attracted to him because he was a dandy sprinter. He did not like the relief camp; he got pretty hot over the thing, and the result was that someone took an interest in him.
2962	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
He went back to the university and is graduating this year in engineering. This shows that these boys will make good if they get a pull in the right direction. The other type of single unemployed is the rural youth, the sons of farmers. They are second to none; they are the cream of the earth-I am one of them.
There are several causes for unemployment. First, we had the crop failures in the west. Then we were faced with continuous unrest in Europe. We have had the accumulation of wealth in the hands of the few, and the introduction of certain types of machinery has displaced labour. But I am convinced that these are not all the real causes. Why is it that in the city of Fort William we have no Hebrews on relief, and no doubt the same thing can be said of other places. They seem to be able to look after their own, while the gentiles apparently cannot measure up in that way. There is one way in which those who hit the highways could be improved If they were encouraged to smoke fewer cigarettes and drink more milk they would have more manhood in them.
The other day someone reminded me of another law, the law of struggle. Any young man or woman who has read natural history, especially zoology, knows that in every form of life a struggle is taking place. Whether it be a kitten, a dog or a youth, once the initiative to fight uphill is lost, the best will not be brought out.
I should like to say a word on behalf of those interested in the distribution of relief. I have not verified this, but I was told by a reputable citizen, a former member of the legislature from Fort William, that two babies that had been raised in homes supported by relief took prizes at a baby show. I go into Fort William to the picture shows and I find them fairly well crowded. I go into the beer parlours and I find a great many people there. People are working to-day who were not working five years ago, yet this problem of unemployment is still with us.
I should like to say something to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) which may perhaps stiffen his vertebrae. Not long ago . a group of youth in Fort William told me to go back and tell the little minister to stick to his job, that he was on the right trail, that he was the first Minister of Labour who had brought in anything in the way of youth training. We are ready to blame the government for everything. There was a great football match being held in England. This was an important match and it was attended by royalty and over 80,000 people. Before the whistle blew it started to rain and one rMr. Mclvor.]
fellow spoke up and said, "This blinking government, why don't they give us a decent day?" But I am not going to blame the government, because I was elected to support the government and I am going to do it. I tell the little Minister of Labour to stick to his job. He has a task worthy of his mettle. We should not forget the advice given by a certain old farmer. This man was greatly depressed because he had no money. Most of his neighbours were in the same position, and he figured out a cure. He said to them, "Put your faith in God, put your back to your work, put your wife in the kitchen and put your car in the garage."

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has been before the house, in the same form almost, for two or three years. I do not intend to speak for more than a few minutes, but I must say that I sympathize with the minister because he has a tiresome, wearisome, thankless job, just as three or four of his predecessors from this side of the house had. However, I believe the text of the resolution and the system are all wrong. We should have a national policy for Canada, adapted to our modern times, in connection with unemployment, but we have never had that. In the United States of America the whole question of unemployment is handled by one man, Mr. Hopkins. In 1927, years before the depression came along, there was presented in that country a report known as the Couzens senate report. This question is not going to be solved by majorities in parliament or parliamentary repartee or wisecracks. Its solution depends on, and calls for broad national service and sacrifice from every man, woman and child in Canada. It will never be solved by half-baked theories or palliatives or patent medicines or quack economic remedies or copious use of the printing presses. If it could, it would have been solved centuries ago.
This problem calls for wide national sacrifices on the part of every man, woman and child in the country. It is true that the government cannot do it all. In my opinion no government can cure unemployment per se. But if the government adopted a forward, courageous, up-to-date, modern policy of wisdom and foresight it would go a long way toward alleviating distress, finding work for the employables and making a better day for unemployables. I do not mean that this whole unemployment question or work should be in connection with public works. The Couzens report, which was issued about twelve years ago, and which made a deep study of

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
it all, stated that public works on a gigantic scale should be undertaken only in times of acute distress. It was contended that expenditures on public works should be left for times of depression, as much as possible, not like here with useless and unnecessary works of a political kind. However, that contention has been found to be not entirely correct as far as the United States is concerned, and was not adopted, but a policy of gigantic public works was adopted there on a wide and ruinous scale.
In my opinion the first thing the minister should do is to change the whole present system. It has been found wanting and Useless. The minister should be divested of a lot of his work. There should be a national committee of this house to consider this problem. Some members of this committee are complaining about the waste of time, but the fact is that we have been here for sixty-eight days, and this is only the fifth or sixth day that we have devoted to the consideration of the problem we were sent here to solve. Any questions that we may deal with between now and May 15, which apparently is to be our closing day, will add little or nothing to the solution of this problem.
The other problems with which we have to deal are interlocked and correlated with this one problem, and if we could have a fair discussion of this problem in a committee of this house I think parliament could conclude its labours very soon. I believe that we should set up a select national committee of this house for the purpose of discussing unemployment questions day by day. Look what the mass buying committee in 1933 and 1934 did for the workers of this dominion. True, it cost S300,000, but it did more for the workers and toilers than any other agency established since confederation. It was the first organization in this country that attempted to bring about some regulation of trade and commerce, the function of this parliament, something which had been ignored and had been the duty of nobody ever since confederation.
Unemployment is not a political question and it never should be. It is a matter of life and death, for if a man loses his job, he might just as well lose his life. It is a question that relates to the life, comfort, health, wealth, peace and prosperity of every citizen of Canada. We should have a labour and employment committee of this house meeting in session and out of session to find jobs for Canadians in Canada. Everybody knows the problem that we had in this house a few years ago of what should be done to provide employment for the returned soldiers, and
we had a pension committee appointed, which has done great work ever since 1935. It has sat as a non-political committee, discussing the questions before it round a table somewhat like the discussion was carried on this afternoon between the Minister of Labour and members on this side. A labour and employment committee such as I have suggested could do a great deal in getting results in regard to the problem of unemployment, in place of a lot of wasteful and useless doomsday commissions.
I believe in showing some ordinary degree of Christian charity towards my political opponents; I always believed in that as a principle of courtesy and respect, and I say to the minister that everybody makes mistakes, every government makes mistakes, and it would be far better to recognize, in this complex question, that a mistake has been made in dealing with unemployment and relief and go back to the old system of dealing directly with the larger municipalities so far as urban and suburban relief is concerned. Ninety per cent of the unemployed, outside agricultural distress, are in the large centres of population, in the big cities. We heard a plea from the conference of mayors along that line the other day. That conference was a great day for Canada. It is time for a change, and I hope the minister will not feel afraid to make a change to a more modem system, because fundamentals are essential. It should have been made long ago.
Under the present system you are forgetting those whom Disraeli called the suffering millions. You allow them to suffer for years from the errors and mistakes that have been made, through the failure to get a coordinated national policy on unemployment. Lord Salisbury once said that the commonest error in politics is sticking to the carcases of dead policies, and that applies particularly to the present system of dealing with unemployment because it is inadequate, inefficient and costly. It is not a long range, national labour policy. It does not avoid the evils of duplication, waste and discrimination. It is not even a national policy in any respect. It has a great many defects and robs collective Peter to pay selective Paul.
Por example, some of the provinces pay nothing towards relief. There is no equality of treatment. In some of the provinces the dominion pays the whole cost of relief for industrial and agricultural workers. Some provinces get assistance with municipal improvements, and other provinces get none. The system is all wrong and should be
2964	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
changed; it is a robber system and should be changed immediately, I am glad to see cities in Quebec province, like Montreal, getting dominion government assistance for parks, playgrounds, schools, sidewalks, roadways and other improvements, but municipalities in Ontario, British Columbia and the maritimes get no assistance of that kind from the federal government, but should get assistance immediately. If the system is wrong let us change it. In Ontario we receive no assistance under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act or little aid from any act, although Ontario pays 42 per cent of all the taxes of Canada. I do plead with the minister not to be afraid to change the present system which has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. Let him unburden himself of a lot of this detailed work and place it where the report of the commission declared it should be-on a national outside commission to adjust it all. The Purvis commission stated that this was a national problem, and assistance should be given by community clubs, boards of trade, with municipalities and the provinces all in it, all doing their part instead of looking to the federal government to handle the whole thing. That is the key to the whole problem. We should have a great national cooperative policy to end unemployment, with everybody in Canada doing his bit, and the present resolution should be amended to that end and the municipalities dealt with directly and not through the provinces.
The federal government deals directly with the municipalities under the farm rehabilitation plan and deals directly with the municipalities in relieving agricultural distress, but in the most important matter of all, unemployment in the industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec this resolution insists on great cities dealing with the provinces. Why should the government not deal with the great tax-paying municipalities directly, justly and liberally? Now in Ontario do we get any assistance under the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act or any just help under any other act? We are the goat of confederation. The present resolution should be amended along the lines I have indicated. There is waste under the present system, favouritism, sectionalism, coma, vacuum and waste, and the system varies in the different provinces according to the way they vote. Some of the provinces pay one-third of the cost of relief and other provinces pay nothing. Some provinces get public and gigantic municipal works and others get nothing. The program of public works should be changed along the lines I have indicated before it is too late.
(Mr. Church.]
Some of the mayors who were in conference in Ottawa recently have been complaining about this very thing. The government in its policy has forgotten the urban workers and the suburban toilers. They are the forgotten men of confederation. The industrial worker is forgotten, with no direct aid.
There are many projects that could be undertaken with benefit to the country and to the unemployed. There is the St. Lawrence waterway. That would be a work of benefit to the country and would provide a large amount of work. The President of the United States is a firm believer in that project. It is the most important work for unemployment. This work will be a feeder to the railways.
In large cities like Toronto and Montreal slum clearance work could be undertaken. Toronto owns its street railway, radial lines and buses, and Montreal has a steam suburban service. Why not start slum clearance as a work measure on trial? There is an opportunity here for providing work through federal assistance in expanding these services. We should also have a national slum clearance and reconstruction policy adapted to our local circumstances at federal expense. We should have had a national register long ago of our man power, our industrial power and our economic power for defence purposes. Canada is criminally neglectful in matters of defence. It is a tragedy.
This country has been getting very little work under the British rearmament program, but just the other day San Francisco got a sixty million dollar contract for the building of aircraft and the United States gets most of the work of this kind. We should have been building storage reservoirs for food; we should have been manufacturing armaments, guns, supplies of various kinds for the British government. We have had a few orders but not nearly enough. A return has been brought down showing that 1,627 industries in this country have been inspected, but very few of them have got any work so far under the British rearmament program. But Australia and the United States have got a great deal.
In Australia, they have built storage reservoirs, and have had large orders for materials for rearmament. Canada has got little or nothing, because of our failure to look for it and our failure to adopt a forward defence and reconstruction policy.
We should have done something long ago towards developing a national coal policy. My national coal policy was adopted ten years ago. Now, in 1938 three million tons of coal have been moved from the maritimes to the head of the lakes economically and has produced a lot of work. We should have a

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
national coal policy that would include also oil and water power, further development all along the line, so as to provide that there will be no power shortage in time of war.
Italy has been carrying out a municipal program of building municipal institutions of all kinds, schools, hospitals and harbours, to provide for her requirements for the next thirty-five years in a municipal way, of all kinds of public local utilities. In Canada we should have a reconstruction, municipal and public utilities policy adapted to our circumstances, and we should also have a national volunteer system of assistance through community clubs, service organizations and the like, all linked up as part of this national employment policy, all coordinated and factors in it.
We are now sitting on the sixty-eighth day of this session. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) has brought down estimates providing for an expenditure of $63,000,000 for defence. Why not let us pass those estimates at once so as to provide work for the unemployed and see that they are spent for militia and real defence? May day is only two weeks off, and the government's program of defence should be accelerated, not only for defence, but to provide a great deal of work all over Canada.
I cannot understand why we can have legislation to provide crop insurance for the prairie provinces and yet have in the industrial provinces no unemployment insurance, which deals with human beings. It is absurd. Why not pass such legislation now? I believe that, as the law clerk of the senate said, and as has been said in the Ontario legislature, under the British North America Act, sec. 91(1), "the public debt and property," parliament can vote any money it likes for federal purposes, especially as all but three of the provinces are willing that it should be done. Never mind constitutional questions; let us act and do things; let us go ahead and do something to develop a policy along the lines which I brought up and referred to on the orders of the day yesterday, and in view of the very forward policy of the Ontario legislature to act at once. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has a policy for ensuring material things, all outside the British North America Act; surely the workers should not be asked to wait any longer for useless commissions and waste of time.
I believe that one of the main causes of unemployment and the accompanying distress in Canada is over-government and over-taxation. Artificial barriers are raised and burdens are put on industry and agriculture to-day which make it almost impossible for a man
successfully to conduct his business, and result in lack of security. The day-to-day conduct of business should be left to those who understand it, and not to a useless lot of professors and dunces. In addition we are handicapped by these favoured nation treaties, the tinkering with the tariffs and useless appeasement treaties. Nothing has been said here about the export of brains to the United States, although some of our ablest young people are going to that country, because of our inaction and incapacity.
A word about the treatment of senior employees, by which I refer to those over forty-five. As I said on this very resolution a year or two ago:
Senior employees, whose lifeblood has been drawn from them by long years of faithful service, are in many cases cast out without retiring allowance to make room for younger and cheaper people. It matters not what suffering is entailed for human beings so long as the stockholders are paid their dividends. This amazing selfishness and shortsightedness of the modern industrial system is creating a progressively lower standard of living and a vicious struggle for existence philosophy on the part of the people, increasingly serious social problems which must find their tragic solution either in war or in revolution. In the face of modern methods of competitive living the royal law of love, bear ye one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ, is a hollow mockery in Canada, presumably a Christian country. This is the contradiction of modern life: a truly wonderful appreciation of the value of the single soul in some quarters, but an absolute denial of any such value in others.
I find in the Couzens report of the United States senate in 1927 a strong recommendation on behalf of senior employees, namely that they should not be exposed to the law of the jungle as in Canada, or the survival of the fittest; for that is what it is-the present system in this country under which men in industrial pursuits cannot get employment when they are over forty-five. What policy has the minister so far as these senior employees are concerned? These senior employees are the forgotten men of Canada. Here is what the Couzens report of 1927 says about these men:
Many of them are still in the prime of life and are able to meet the requirements of industry. They are not old in the sense that they have outgrown their usefulness. Yet once they have been discharged they find it exceedingly difficult to secure new employment. It is the duty of American industry to keep these men on their payrolls rather than to turn them adrift upon a labour market which refuses to absorb, their services.
I believe further that the industries of this country, owing to the tariff tinkering and the useless trade treaties, are not getting a fair show and are being ruined. There are now no industries working on full time in Canada,
2966	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
but who could be but for these wide tariff surrenders. The Couzens report indicates a situation due largely to changes in the tariff when it says, at page 495:
To say that all industries are seasonal would hardly be an exaggeration. It would be most difficult to find an industry which showed an even distribution of production and employment throughout the year. An individual plant, here and there to be sure, may show steady and regular employment from month to month, but such plants are exceptions and by no means the rule in any industry.
That was a report of prophecy. Now in 1939, so far as Canada is concerned with the loss of our home markets, so much for the consequences of tariff tinkering and that sort of thing.
There should be some amendment of the law with respect to treatment of transients and other unemployed. The gaols of this country are being filled with these young people. I recently referred to the situation at Toronto, Timmins and other centres, and the comments of judges and magistrates, and I have read in this chamber what the magistrates have said, that these men are in prison not for any crime but because of inability to find a job. The Vagrancy Act should be amended so that men who are looking for work and doing no wrong should not be held in detention as they are under the present law. Let us grasp the cause and effect of it all in a Christian country. Yesterday the hon. member for Wellington North said that nobody wanted to go back to the farm. As far as I can find out there is no work, or at any rate very little, on the farm. I spoke a month ago on "waste not, want not," and of the inroads of the machine. The machine has taken the place of human labour, on the farms and prairies, with results which are evident not only on the prairies but in all parts of the country and in all parts of the world. As far as that is concerned we should have a forward policy, not only for agriculture but for other industries and to help the forgotten man, the industrial worker. Little or nothing has been done.
At page 10 of the Purvis report reference is made to what can be done for casual unemployment by an increase of the tourist trade. The departmental stores take advantage of that situation; the coming of their majesties is made an occasion in the United States for providing a good deal of casual work, but here we have no national policy and the people are not prepared to take advantage of these opportunities, or prepare the way for this glorious visit or educate the school children, as they did in France last July, as to the king and queen and all the monarchy stands for.

The time has come to return to the old system of dealing with the large municipality directly, who pay most of the cash taxes, and encouraging the apprenticeship system. In Canada apprenticeship is only in its infancy; our school boards and industrialists should help; we have not adopted the system they have in England; we are not providing any national system of training for either peace or war. We are asleep; we are not interested in establishing a proper plan of cadet and national training in camps for youth in the summer or all the year around on the lines which I described a few weeks ago as having been adopted in England, where they take the unemployed, provide work, clothing, food and lodging for them with some pay, give them physical drill, and prepare them to learn a trade, so that at the end of three or four years they can get jobs in the air force or as mechanics in industrial establishments. By such methods we should be preparing for defence and for industrial and defence training. To-day we are standing at the parting of the ways. As Adam Smith said, security is better than opulence. A great deal of voluntary training of those who want to get on and sign up, and a real education, could be undertaken under a national program of the kind I have indicated, which has met with great success in England and in France and aids defence, employment for the future, and real national service and patriotism. Let us reduce unemployment by preparing for adequate defence not only on land but at sea and in the air all along the British and French lines. What is the government doing about the submarine menace, about the menace of aircraft, about the defence of the civilian population? Absolutely nothing, and giving no leadership. Surely it has some program along these lines or should have before the enemy come here. We are criminally negligent as to defence.
Rearmament will provide work, and I hope that the Minister of National Defence, who I believe has a good program ready, which will be taken up in the next few days, will be able to provide a good deal of employment before May day, and real help to our faithful militia. I doubt whether there will be a great deal of discussion of his proposals, in view of the long debate we have already had, but, with May day coming, very soon a day should be set apart to deal with this problem immediately and defend Canada before it is too late. I hope that when the government come to it they will have a national policy of employment and defence for the youth of this country, conceived along

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
the lines of a volunteer system absolutely, for these out of work, with pay, especially in the summer time, when students at the high schools can go to these camps and be educated for duty, patriotism and service and receive pay and education in patriotism and trade. Since when did it become a crime for a man to defend his country? I believe that a scheme of this national kind can be developed to an extent where a great deal of various kinds of unemployment would be taken care of, particularly among employable youths around eighteen years of age or a little over, as has been done in England, for youths, with pay, training and board. The matter should be taken up and considered at once by the government on a volunteer basis.
That is all I have to say. I am sorry to have detained the committee, but parliament has been sitting for sixty-eight days and this subject has been under discussion for only five days. I believe that when it is disposed of, because there are so many problems correlated with it, we may hope to see soon the end of the session.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yesterday I rose to
speak briefly in this debate because I felt that a group of the younger people had been misrepresented in this chamber. To-night there are one or two other matters to which I wish to refer briefly. The first is that I regret that this year again we are discussing a resolution foreshadowing much the same kind of measure to deal with unemployment and agricultural aid that we have had before us in preceding years. The legislation expires annually on March* 31, I believe, and new agreements have to be made each year with the several provinces. It is, therefore, a purely temporary policy that we are again discussing. I would say to the minister I believe that we ought to be considering a long-term policy, because, as has been suggested from all sides of the house, this problem is no longer an emergency one, but one which we have had with us for a long time and are likely to have for a long time yet. I noted that when the brief was presented to the minister by the youth of this country some time ago, that opinion was stated very clearly. And the young Canadians who presented that brief on behalf of themselves and others in the same position were anxious that something should
be done not only to meet the contingency of the moment but to provide at least some measure of solution for the problem that they face in the future. Therefore it seems to me that parliament is not justified in passing this resolution, towards the end of the fourth session of this parliament, merely to continue the kind of annual policy that we have had in the past. I do not agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that the attitude of the house generally is one of indifference; I do not think it is. I think the attitude of hon, members on all sides is more or less one of troubled consideration, if I may put it in that way.
Ever since 1929 unemployment has been with us in an acute form. To-day instead of being acute, one might almost be justified in describing it as chronic. In 1930 the hon. gentlemen who occupy office to-day, members of the Liberal party, were defeated because of the growing discontent and unemployment all across the country. The government of that time refused to recognize the problem as a national one, believing it could be dealt with by the municipalities and the provinces. As I said, the government of that time was defeated, and the Conservatives came into power with the promise that the problem would be considered as a national one and an attempt made to solve it by various national measures. We know that they also failed. Now it seems to me that in the fourth session of this parliament, this government, although having an overwhelming majority behind them, are also failing to meet this pressing problem of unemployment.
Yesterday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) spoke of the necessity of solving this problem because it endangered the system under which we live. I should like to quote his words as reported at page 2911 of yesterday's Hansard:
I believe that the system under which we are living, the capitalistic system, the democratic system, is the best system, a system worthy of preservation, and I want to preserve it;
My reading of history teaches me that society continually evolves. At the present time we are evolving from what we may call the competitive system to a cooperative society. In some respects that evolution accounts for some of the probelms we are facing to-day; in other words, we are witnessing the break-down more or less of the old system and the troubled birth of a new one. Believing as I do in evolution and orderly progress, I am afraid that, if this progress is obstructed, it will result in even more discontent and in uprisings which in the end may
2968	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
bring about something in the way of a revolution. And I do not like to contemplate either a revolution from the extreme right, which we to-day call fascism, or a revolution from the extreme left which is sometimes spoken of as communism.
The leader of the opposition yesterday spoke of capitalism and democracy as though the terms were synonymous. Perhaps they once were. But now the monopolies which we find within capitalism, which cause unemployment, and discontent, resulting in the kind of regimentation that we have in relief administration, actually destroy the democracy which we once knew. Because I believe firmly in democracy I have no confidence in a system which undermines our political democracy and perhaps makes economic democracy impossible. Yet because I do believe in evolution I believe that we should do all we can to preserve that which is good in the present system and to eliminate the evil, 3ecau.se in that way we are really laying the rest kind of foundation for the society that nust be built.
In our country at the moment the two most rressing problems, which in some degree are embodied in the resolution presented by the minister, are unemployment and the plight of agriculture. It seems to me that we cannot separate the one from the other. They are interrelated, and neither of them can be cured by the kind of policy that we have pursued, that of maintaining people on relief at relatively low levels of existence, because relief ultimately undermines those who receive it. Let me interject, you cannot cure the problem of agriculture by reducing the farmer to the level of the European peasant, and that is what the government's proposals regarding wheat marketing will really do if they are carried out in their present form.
What I said yesterday I repeat to-night; that parliament ought not to prorogue or adjourn until these problems have been tackled in a much more satisfactory manner than they have been up to the present time. None of us wishes to remain here during the heat of the summer. It seems to me, however, that we in this house would not be doing our duty at the present time if we did not endeavour to impress upon the government the necessity of doing something really worth while in connection with these problems. May I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that two years ago we had a very short session; parliament prorogued early in order that hon. members might attend the ceremonies in connection with the coronation, and it seems to me the people of this country would feel that

we had not fulfilled our duties as a parliament if we did not give more consideration to these problems than they are receiving at the present time.
Last night the hon. member for Yukon (Mrs. Black) said she had heard no constructive suggestions to deal with these pressing problems. I think, as a matter of fact, suggestions have come from time to time from all quarters of this house, irrespective of party. Speaking for the group with which I am connected I would say that we have seldom risen to criticize a government measure or policy without offering at least some constructive proposal which, in our opinion, was worth presenting to this parliament.
Before sitting down I should like to enumerate some of the proposals we have made at various times and to say that long before 1929 members now connected with this group urged preparation for the cyclical unemployment which has been witnessed from time to time under the present economic system. As early as 1922 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) proposed in this house that a system of unemployment insurance should be established. I have before me at the moment a long list of resolutions, which I do not propose to read, which have been moved in the house by members of this group on various occasions. As I have said, in 1922 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre introduced a resolution advocating unemployment insurance. In 1926, to pick some out at random, the same hon. member moved a motion that unemployment insurance should be established. In 1929- and in the intervening years similar resolutions were moved-the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) moved that all provinces be requested to pass unemployment insurance legislation, because of the constitutional difficulty that then existed. In the 1930 session the same hon. member moved that the house discuss the serious unemployment problem that existed throughout the country, and the debate lasted for six days. I am not going to mention all the resolutions that were moved, but other members of the house suggesting similar action have always received the support of the group with which I am associated.
When the problem became acute, following 1929, the members of our group made many suggestions, including public works programs, housing, reforestation, irrigation, road building and so on. Again and again these suggestions were urged, and again and again the government was asked to recognize the necessity of making preparation to finance these undertakings. Time after time this group urged

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
upon the government the necessity of establishing a central bank in order to make currency and credit an instrument of national policy. We have suggested that chartered banks actually engaged in the loan business should be brought more closely under government control, that investments should be directed, and so on. All those things had to do with answering the question as to where the funds would come from to finance these undertakings. Then, in order to distribute purchasing power to the agricultural community, we have constantly urged that adequate marketing legislation should be placed on the statute books and that reasonable minimum prices should be fixed for farm products.
Then, to create opportunities for youth, we suggested that the age limit for old age pensions should be lowered and the amount of the pensions increased, in order that people might be encouraged to retire. After all, opportunities must be found for our young people. As I said yesterday, while the condition of those in middle age is deplorable, much more regrettable is the condition of the young people. When I cross the line and see the splendid work that is being done in the CCC. camps, under the WPA. programs and so on in the United States, I only wish we might do something of that kind for the youth of our country. But when people speak of camps in Canada, of course some immediately say all we need do is place our young people under military discipline. My observation of the civilian camps in the United States has convinced me that there is no military discipline there. As a matter of fact they do use some of the military terms and titles, but they have a free and easy self-discipline which, in my opinion, is a good type of discipline for our young people.

So far as we are concerned, our object in discussing this matter at the present time is to endeavour, if we can, to move the government from its complacency. It seems to be too satisfied with the condition which exists in Canada, and yet all across the country there is a rising tide of discontent.
There is much more one might say, but I do not wish to prolong the discussion tonight. I rise simply because I wish first of all to state that in my opinion this policy of going on from year to year, from April 1, to March 31, with a condition which is becoming chronic in our midst, is not good enough and not wise enough for the wellbeing of the country in which we live.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to detain the committee very long. However, there are two aspects of the case to which I should like to direct attention. Last Friday I had not time to do so.
First of all, I should like to point out the excellent studies which have been made by the Canadian welfare council with regard to the problem of the non-resident and migrant. May I be permitted to read a brief extract which seems to me to summarize the situation :
And so, we come, surely, to a realization that both in its social and in its legal aspects we are face to face with a problem existent long prior to the present depression. Looking at it frankly we can gauge its potential extent by the fact that practically a third of the gainfully occupied population of Canada is engaged in the primary activities which chiefly feed it.
Some of the registration statistics, issued by the national employment commission, indicated that even at its lowest level, our non-resident and homeless men must have exceeded 50,000: doubtless the total has been as high as 100,000 at some times. Only those who are accepted as in receipt of aid as individuals in some one centre are registered, and the general experience of our larger centres (possibly a fair reflex of the movement through the smaller towns and cities), is that from a quarter to a third of the number aided at any time are non-resident. The more mobile elements in these groups are not likely to be stationary, unless in the depth of winter, for the one constant factor in local policy in many centres is to keep these men moving.
As we look back upon the decades of this century in Canada's story, in the light of our experience of these immediate years, we can see the situation in a three-pronged challenge to our progress.
1.	The problem of assuring gainful occupation on a self-supporting basis for a large supply of necessarily mobile and necessarily young labour;
2.	The problem of assuring reasonable social care for these men whose very modes of life have defeated marriage and the establishment of homes; and
3.	The problem of tying down both employment and social care facilities on a basis of residence.
Let us accept the common starting point that, for this body of thousands of potential workers and other thousands who are "burned out," our primary interest is in man power or the care of men, rather than in the fixing or shifting of maintenance costs. If we do so, we must admit that our first objective should be to stop the wandering tide and to make the acquisition of settlement or residence, somewhere, possible. Only by such action can we arrive at the sorting out of the human atoms now adrift. Then we

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
can effect the reestablishment of those who have homes and residence, somewhere, and for whom reestablishment offers there, and we can sort out the others into those who can be salvaged for self-supporting occupation and those who may have to become social charges on a more or less permanent basis. The line of solution will follow the natural outline of the problem itself in its legal and its social aspects.
I shall not take the time of the committee to elaborate upon these statements, or to comment upon them, or to quote further from the other excellent pamphlets which have been published by the Canadian welfare council. I would, however, urge that the government has been amply supplied with the facts in the case and with careful studies which should enable it to carry out a reconstruction program. The whole matter comes back, it seems to me, to the willingness of the government to undertake this work. The only reason why we should prolong for a moment the debate at this time is to insist on behalf of a large number of the unemployed that the country as a whole expects the government to take action along these lines.
