The third document came to me just recently from another organization-I am not familiar with Saint John-which calls itself the family welfare association of Saint John. This is a report of a survey of families on relief, and I shall read only a few paragraphs:
The 200 or more special visits made on this survey covered a cross section of the most depressed areas. The findings from these visits may be summarized as follows:-
A great many of the families were living in quarters actually unfit for human habitation; there was also overcrowding, suffering from cold, lack of clothing, bedding, cooking utensils and food.
There was plain evidence of slow starvation among many adults and little children in this group, and the ravages of diseases were apparent as attested by their medical and hospital records.
Most of these homes were without bed sheets or towels and had less than half enough other bedding.
Some families had one bed for the family and no mattress; a large number of this group of families had exhausted supplies of cooking utensils and in some homes one pot was used for cooking and bottles for drinking, in absence of cups.
In the remainder of the cases visited, the majority revealed evidence of considerable hardship with undernourishment and the results had affected a number of children. In almost every ease visited, the family were existing very much below the minimum standard of decent living and without enough food or clothing.
And further on:
Seventy-five per cent of the families owe from three to sixteen months' rent. Most housing conditions are squalid and unsanitary; a terrible lack of clothing, bedding and utensils. A large section of those visited had been evicted from three to six times a year. During the past two years, fifty per cent of these families had moved from three to twelve times.
And again:
Slightly over fifty per cent have suffered from ill-health and had hospital treatment during the last two years, having had from one to six members of the family in hospital at different times. According to a recent report by the district medical health officer on conditions, this was due because "undernourishment, insufficient or inadequate food, acute and chronic illnesses, and poor hygienic conditions, have existed so long a time in the community that they are now presenting a most serious economic problem."

Most of the families suffer from a deficiency of milk. Milk used is principally canned and averages a few cans a week per family.
The clothing scarcity is marked. Many children are unable to leave the homes or attend school for lack of clothing. Red cross, churches and other organizations and private individuals have assisted to the limit, but the requirements far exceed the supply.
Taking five family cases of the group mentioned, we quote as follows from the survey reports:-
Family-north end. Two adults and one child five months of age. Behind in rent, little bedding. Man active tuberculosis case, has no underwear, socks or overcoat. Relief $1.50 per week-extra $1.25 per week from church.
Family-west end. One adult and three children from seven to nine years of age. Owe one year's rent. Beds and mattresses in bad condition, no sheets, no towels, no fresh milk obtainable. All children in one bed to keep warm. House cold. Neighbours have to provide ferry tickets to enable woman to work for relief of $2 per week at the Red Cross sewing centre.
Family-south end. Two adults and seven children from three to eighteen years. Owe eleven months' rent. Beds, clothing in bad condition. Eighteen year old girl is ill. Bad cases of undernourishment. $5.60 per week in relief.
Family-east end. Two adults and eight children from one and one-half to fourteen years. Owe six months' rent. One bed, no mattress. Bedding almost nil. No cups. Man in hospital and consequently relief order had to be reduced to $3.20 per week. Very bad conditions here.
Family-north end. Two adults and two children, ten and thirteen years. House cold, girl just had mastoid operation, sleeps on mattress on the floor; no fresh milk. House perfectly awful. No quilts, wretched clothing. Relief $3.50 per week.
These cases are average of 210 surveyed.
There are many relief regulations which no doubt appear necessary but which are disastrous to family life, i.e., in case of the arrest of the head of the house, family can now only receive municipal help by going to the poor house. As this includes children the effects are very bad. In the past, relief works orders could be obtained in such cases by the wife working for the order.
If either husband or wife in a family is in receipt of an old age pension the remainder of the family become ineligible for work relief. This is a great hardship.
We find that many men on work relief, exposed to the most severe weather had thin clothing and no underwear. Consequently some became ill and were cared for at municipal cost through the hospital. The hospital expenses exceeded the cost of proper clothing.
From records of families on relief and those in a similar condition not on relief, there is evidence that there must be one thousand families in Saint John in greatly depressed circumstances, unable to gain the meanest living in employment, without assistance. In nearly every case the head of the family states that inability to secure work has forced them into this situation although there are quite a few widows, and others who have suffered illness or injuries.

I am not going to prolong this discussion. We are having an example right now of the arbitrary, almost callous disregard of Canadian people and, my friend here suggests, by the Liberal party.
I do not say that individually the members of the Liberal party are any worse than other people. But I do say that the Liberal party constitutes the government of this country and they are the people who have to accept the responsibility. There is no use in my talking to Conservatives or other parties in this house. The question was asked in the most casual way, just as though the hon. member were talking about an eclipse of the moon or something like that, without the slightest bit of feeling or the slightest evidence of any desire to get to the essential needs of these unemployed.
Let me tell my hon. friend that I meet the unemployed fairly often, and every time I meet them I feel ashamed. I see the things they are wearing for shoes; instinctively I look at my own, because I wear fairly decent shoes. I look at their clothes and then instinctively I look at my own and feel ashamed. What right have I, what right have you to something thousands of others in the community do not have? I should like to tell my hon. friend that the wealth of the world to-day is a social product, brought forth by the combined efforts of all those whom we allow to participate in its production.
Take, for example, the production of wheat, about which we hear so much these days. Actually the farmer in western Canada does not produce wheat; he plays a part in its production. Before he can produce wheat at all, a great many things must take place. In the first place men must go down into the bowels of the earth and take out iron ore. Other men must go down into the bowels of the earth and take out coal. These two commodities are brought together; we have pig iron, then iron, then steel. These materials go through various processes in the factories and agricultural machinery is produced, after which it is transported to the farms. Then the farmer uses it to plant his seed, to reap and thresh his crop, which then has to be transported to where it is consumed. The product is not finally produced until it reaches the ultimate consumer. Before and after the farmer contributes his share, hundreds of thousands of other people-the whole of society-take some part in the production of this commodity. Then we find manipulators on the grain exchange, who possibly would not know a grain of wheat from a grain of oats, who never contributed one day's labour to the production of this commodity, but who live bountifully while the

farmer and many of the others who worked to produce those crops go around with the seats out of their pants.

I have told hon. members until I am tired of telling them, that we are faced with a condition which requires a fundamental change in the economic and social set-up of society itself. What is a government? Is it not an instrument formed by the people to do for them collectively what they are not able to do for themselves individually? If we have allowed the means of production in this country to get into the hands of a few people who take the cream of the wealth and leave the great mass of the people in poverty, then the function of government is to see to it that the wealth produced by the people is restored to the people in order that they may have it to meet their need.

speechtext:
Is that any reason why I should not know how the workers live? I have worked for hire, and if that is not the way to find out, then I should like to know how to find it out. Who should know better whether or not I can live on my wage-I or my employer? The hon. member has been so accustomed to taking the employer's word for things that he would not know a worker if he met one on the street-not if he could possibly pass him by without taking notice of him.
I have before me a statement which gives a good picture of the way in which we deal with people on relief. I believe my own province of British Columbia has as good relief arrangements as are to be found anywhere in Canada. The average cost for relief for a child in that province-and a child is any person from a day old to the age of twenty-one years-is 15-83 cents a day.
Probably I should say that this compilation of figures has been made by a person who has taken a great interest in governmental institutions in British Columbia-a member of the provincial legislature. If the father dies the mother gets the mother's
pension or mother's allowance until the child is sixteen years of age. The allowance for the child is 24-66 cents a day. If the mother dies and the child becomes the ward of the Children's Aid Society, the child costs the state or the province, whichever you like, 73-4 cents a day. If the mother lives, the child upon reaching the age of sixteen years goes back on relief and gets 15-83 cents a day.
If a boy gets into trouble and is sent to an industrial school, it costs the state $2.19 a day to look after him. If it is a girl and she is sent to the girls' industrial school, it costs the state $1.64 a day to look after her. Or, if the child is still a child on relief, but is a little older, he goes to the provincial gaol at a cost to the province of 91 cents a day. Later on, if he gets into more trouble, he qualifies for the penitentiary and his keep costs the state $2.59 a day.
Then he is released from the penitentiary at the age of twenty, or before he is twenty-one, and he goes back again on relief at 15-83 cents a day-although in the penitentiary it had cost the government $2.59 a day to keep him. Then, after he reaches his twenty-first birthday, if he is still out of work and on relief, it costs the state 42 cents a day. He may remain on that until he reaches old age, when he would go to an old men's home in Vancouver at a cost to the government of 64 cents a day. If he were to go to the old people's home at Kamloops he would cost the government 89 cents a day. If he went to the infirmary for incurables he would cost the government $1.32 a day. If he received an old age pension he would cost the government 65f cents a day.
If, during all these difficulties, he should contract tuberculosis he would be sent to Tranquille sanatorium at a cost to the government of $2.47 a day. If he contracted some other acute illness he would be sent to the Vancouver general hospital at a cost of $3.71 a day.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: The hon. member stated a moment ago that unemployment should be dealt with as an emergency. Then he stated it was no longer an emergency, but was going to remain with us-I take it he meant that it will remain permanently. Would he, then, subscribe to the statement that there is no cure for it-if he states it is a permanent thing?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: No, I cannot say that there is no cure for it. As a matter of fact it is not unemployment itself that is bad. What is wrong is the condition of being unemployed without income. I know of a great many people who are unemployed and enjoy it. They can go south in the winter and go to the mountains in the summer. They are having a whale of a time, and they are unemployed all the time-that is, provided they cannot find some diversion which will occupy their time. What is required is not the ending of unemployment, but rather the provision of access to the means of production or the means of existence for the people, so that with the proper exercise of their own efforts they can live as well as the resources of the country will permit. I do not see any reason in the world why a cabinet minister, a member of parliament, a judge, a deputy minister, a life insurance president or anyone else, simply because he happens to be in a more advantageous position and has a pull on a bigger share of the national income, should have an assured income while other people have to go without any income at all.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

Abraham replied "They have Moses and the prophets. If they believe not them, neither would they believe, even though one rose from the dead." I am afraid my hon. friends are very much in the position of Dives.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext: I am really interested in the remarks of the hon. gentleman and I should like to ask him a question. Does he consider it to be a part of the function of government that every citizen or individual in the country should be assured an income?

speechtext: It is susceptible of being answered by yes or no, and I say "yes." Otherwise what is government for?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Apparently my hon. friend was asleep, so I shall have to say it again. It is the duty of government to see that every person in the country willing to work under decent conditions and to assume his share of the obligations of the country is assured an income adequate to his needs. That is my reply to the question asked by my hon. friend. The government is organized to do quite a number of things, and it will have to do many more things. The government is doing dozens of things to-day which would have been considered rank socialism if they had been even suggested twenty years ago. That applies not only to this country but to other countries throughout the world. But it is only in those countries where they have done these things in a planned way that real progress is being made.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Which countries?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) referred on several occasions to New Zealand, Sweden and Denmark, and there are other small countries with the same kind of government. These countries have definitely accepted the principle that the function of government is to assure the economic and social welfare of their people. We in Canada are accepting *this responsibility reluctantly, hesitatingly and in a very small measure. Consider the bills now on the order paper sponsored by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and by other ministers. Every one of them is on the order paper because of the failure of private industry-that is industry operating without government aid-to enable people to make a living.
I have before me a clipping from the Vancouver Daily Province of October 7, 1935, reporting a speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in Barrie on the same date. Referring to the former government and its difficulties with provincial governments, the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
"Mr. Bennett had called a few provincial conferences," said Mr. King, "but they had lasted only a few days and the procedings consisted only in a lecture from Mr. Bennett." The one he personally proposed would remain at work until an agreement was reached on every problem in which both provinces and dominion had any common interests.
That was just a week before the election of 1935, and the Prime Minister and his party were elected on those promises. As I said a little earlier, they accepted unemployment as the most urgent national problem and as a matter concerning the provincial and federal governments and requiring the attention of both. Mr. Bennett was not highly successful with his provincial conferences, but the Prime Minister went up and down this country telling the people how successful he would be with his. He was going to call a conference which would be the last because it would clear up all the difficulties. Of course, at the present time Mr. Hepburn and other good Liberals-if there are any-appear to be of a different mind. The feeling is not so cooperative in certain provinces as the Prime Minister would like it to be.
Just one other word. We are asked to cooperate. Ever since this government came into power, during the last parliament and ever since this group has been represented in this House of Commons, there has never been a constructive proposal submitted which has not received our support. The difficulty we find in cooperating is that the government submits practically nothing for us to cooperate on. I was not present when the vote was taken on the last trade treaty, but the other members of this group who were here voted in favour of that treaty. We voted with the government on the trade agreement of 1936. I would point out further that we voted against the Ottawa agreements because we felt that while from the narrow point of view they might be of benefit to this country, ultimately they would not be of benefit because they made world trade more difficult.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I wish to say a few words in refutation of the statements that have been made to-night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) because I feel I should be remiss in my duty if I allowed the house and the country to think that Saint John is in the condition in which he reported it to be. speechtext:
Do 1 understand
the hon. member to say that these statements from the family welfare association are incor-reot?

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
Speaking from the point of view of the manufacturers, I think our people in Saint John have done their best to keep their workmen going. They have done so through hard times, they are doing so to-day, and will continue to do their best. I think the hon. member for Beauce has done his best to keep the pulp mill in Saint John going. I submit that the situation in Saint John as represented by the statements which have been read in the house to-night has been grossly exaggerated.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

I know them all very
well, but I still submit that the picture was not presented in its proper light. There are a few families in distress, but the picture is not as was presented to-night. Cases of distress can be found in every city throughout Canada, and conditions in Saint John are no worse than in other cities; in fact, they are slightly better.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I desire to refer to the
recommendations of the Canadian welfare council for the purpose of basing on them certain questions with regard to the plans of the government respecting the transient or non-resident unemployed. I think it is generally agreed that lack of uniformity in residential qualifications across Canada has seriously aggravated the situation. That is chiefly the reason why British Columbia has been required to shoulder more than its just share of the burden with regard to transients. No one can accuse the welfare council of having overstated or exaggerated conditions. If I interpret their study of this question aright, it is essentially a plea for a different approach to the question, that we should regard these men not so much as a liability to be sidestepped by shifting the responsibility, but rather as an asset to be conserved and developed. The welfare council in a booklet entitled, Wayfarers Perforce, states in a prefatory note:
These suggestions represent merely the best thought which it has been possible to garner on this problem, and are submitted as such for the consideration of the respective governments.
They go on to say, under the heading of "Need for uniformity in residence rules":
It is recognized that any principles governing residence should progressively be made uniform, not only as between municipalities within a province, through intra-provincial legislation, but also as between differing provincial jurisdictions under some form of interprovincial agreement, or under conditions which the dominion government might attach to its grants-in-aid agreements with the provinces, under the Unemployment and Agricultural Assistance Act. It is also recognized that, in addition to obtaining uniformity of residence rules between different areas, municipal or provincial, for purposes of aid to which the dominion government contributes, there is the further problem of making these uniform residence or settlement rules applicable to all forms of social assistance within each province.
They go on to say in another paragraph:
Before endeavouring to agree upon any actual definition of residence that might be set forth in provincial or interprovincial agreements, it would seem that the fundamental principle must he laid down that, whatever the definition of residence, no person who has established a residence in any province or local area, under any definition of the term, should lose that residence until he has established residence elsewhere.
The council then goes on to give what is called their program in summary, which they have submitted to the government, the first part of which I read the other evening. Part II refers to the liability of the dominion and suggests acceptance by the dominion government of responsibility for certain things:
The acceptance by the dominion government of responsibility for
(1)	taking steps to obtain the establishment, on the basis of uniform residence rules, of the four following generally accepted classifications on the basis of residence;
(a)	local residents, those belonging to some municipal area within a province;
(b)	provincial residents, those belonging to no local area within a province but to the province as a whole;
(c)	inter-provincial residents, namely those with residence in some provincial area or subdivision of it other than the province where they find themselves in need;
(d)	migrants, or those who cannot be shown to have established residence in any province under any generally acceptable definition of residence but who have moved about from province to province in such a way as to be deprived of residence anywhere;
(2)	arbitration facilities for the adjustment of conflicting claims among provinces in respect to the establishment of residence claims for persons whose residence may be in dispute among different provinces;
(3)	assuring proper provisions, until legal residence can he acquired, for the residual number of persons who may have lost legal residence in any one province, or who, having drifted in and out of Canada, are found to be migrants or casuals without place of fixed abode, or the possibility of early establishing one.
III. As the joint liability of citizens and government.

(1)	the creation of central registry bureaux at all probable centres of heavy concentration of non-resident or migrant persons;
(2)	the issuance of a special credential card *which will enable the bearer at all times to prove his place of established legal residence, or his interim status, while acquiring residence;
(3)	the withdrawal, to more or less permanent care through farm hostels and similar plans, of all persons obviously incapable ot reestablishment on a self-supporting basis;

(6)	every effort, within the local community, and on the part of the private employer, to develop occupational opportunities for workers, enrolling in the special training or rvork projects.
I now come to the minister's words, which appear at page 224 of Hansard, of January 23, 1939, when he is speaking of grants in aid.
He says:
Under the proposed agreements the dominion government will provide for a sharing of the cost of aid given to transients on a fifty-fifty basis with the province.
Mv first question to the minister is this: Is there any objection or any obstacle that cannot now be overcome with regard to the acceptance of these recommendations making for uniformity of residential rights across the dominion? Second, is it his intention under the proposed agreements,' to which I have made reference, to define more clearly residential qualifications on a uniform basis across the dominion? I think this is important because everyone agrees that existing conditions are seriously aggravating the problem of transients.
'Mr. ROGERS: As to the first question, it was announced on January 23 that the dominion government was prepared to join with the provinces in sharing the cost of relief given to transients. The implementation of that undertaking will require an agreed definition of " transients," and that in turn will probably require some uniformity among the provinces with respect to the rules governing domicile. At the present time that uniformity does not exist. Our present negotiations with the provinces for an agreement covering this fiscal year will tend, we
[Mr. MacNeil.J

There were four recommendations along these lines in the report of the national employment commission. May I read them?
1.	Establishment of definitions of residence on a comparable basis all across Canada.
2.	Reciprocal basis of maintenance and reimbursement among different units of administration in respect to those aided in a unit other than their own.

4.	Establishment of central bureaux for the "clearing" of non-resident and migrant applications in certain large centres of known concentration.
That is included in the report of the commission in October, 1937. Has anything been done to implement those four recommendations? They will be found at page 89 of the report.

As a matter of fact, if my hon. friend examines those recommendations he will find that a number of them can be carried into effect only by action of the provinces. ourselves cannot correct that situation. There is also a reference to reciprocal arrangements. In respect to_ the first-the legal, technical problem of residence, the commission recommended-

I wish to say a few words with reference to unemployment in New Brunswick. I had not intended to say anything, but the matter was brought up to-night. Speaking generally, I think I can truthfully

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
say that unemployment in New Brunswick has been greatly on the increase during the past year. That is on account of the fact that there has not been much lumbering there during the past winter, especially on the north shore and up the Miramichi river. In my own town of Sussex I know that during the nine years of the depression the situation has not been worse than it is at the present time.
With reference to Saint John I am, of course, not as well acquainted with that city as is the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. McAvity), but if it were possible for him to improve conditions in Saint John I am sure he would. I know that the situation in the port this last winter has been one of the worst we have had in many years. As to the cause of that condition we may have different ideas, but I know the longshoremen in Saint John believe that the reason why there has been so little work in that port this winter is the recent trade agreements which we have made with the United States and Great Britain. In past winter many millions of bushels of wheat went through the port of Saint John, this winter there has been very little, and I think that what is true of Saint John is also true of the port of Halifax.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Saint John-Albert say that he believed the statement read by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was grossly exaggerated. I know the men who signed their names to that report; they are responsible men in Saint John. Mr. Anglin is one of the leading barristers of that city, W. Usher Miller is secretary of the Protestant orphanage and as such is brought into contact with conditions there and charitable work almost daily. Reverend W. C. V. Martin has also been extensively connected with welfare work in Saint John, and I know no one who would be more responsible in making a report than Reverend Mr. Martin. I could not let go unchallenged the statement that these men exaggerated conditions there. And Inspector McLeese who, with another man, is reported as having made a statement in the Saint John Times is a member of the Saint John police force, part of his duty as inspector being, I understand, to visit the homes and look after the giving of relief and other such matters. So I believe that the statement made by these men is correct, that they are responsible men and, I am satisfied, would not in any way exaggerate a matter of this kind.

It is impossible to give the committee at this time the precise allocation of this amount among the various provinces. As a matter of fact, a considerable part of this item is usually reserved for the winter months, when the problem of the special care of single unemployed is increased.
How does the minister make up the item if he does not know what work is to be carried on?

We do have some idea of what work is to be carried on. For instance, we have always made provision for the farm employment plan in British Columbia, although they have only placed a small number, I believe two or three hundred being the maximum. Then in cooperation with the province we have operated forest conservation camps, generally during the winter months. As a rule these camps are opened in the middle of October and are closed some time in April or May.
Were they not operated by the provincial government?
They are administered by the provincial government under an agreement with the dominion government, the cost being shared equally by the two governments.
Does the minister intend to enter into agreements similar to those he entered into with the provinces in connection with the farm placement plan?

That will be subject to negotiations in the early autumn with the provincial governments concerned. That has

Did the minister give the figures in connection with farm placements for this year and previous years?
On April 10 of this year the number on placement in Manitoba was 9,069. In April of last year the number was 9,350.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to paragraph (a) of section 1 of the agreement entered into last year between the dominion and the Alberta government. Dealing with this matter as a municipal official, I must say that I consider this clause to be rather severe. It reads:
The total of all amounts paid by the province to farmers, resident in the province, for taking into and maintaining in residence and in their employment, during the aforesaid period, any of the individuals described in the next succeeding subsection hereof as eligible to receive payment thereunder who were, immediately prior to such employment registered in any of the cities of Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat or Drumheller as single, homeless unemployed, it being understood that the maximum amount to which the dominion will contribute in respect of any of said farmers hereunder shall not exceed the rate of five dollars per month for each of said individuals so taken into and maintained in employment.
I should like the minister to reconsider this section. There were a number of young men who had been working on farms but who found themselves out of work. When they went to a municipal office in order to be put under the scheme, they were told that the only way whereby they could qualify was to go to Edmonton, Calgary, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat or Drumheller and register. I suggest that the minister consider modifying this sec>
tion to make it agree with the terms in the agreement of 1937, and leave the discretion with the municipal officials as to whether or not cases are just and proper.

The change in the Alberta agreement was made at the request of the provincial government. The dominion government tries to cooperate with the provinces in connection with any special arrangements which they may feel are necessary in order to meet their own situation. This particular request was made to us by the provincial government.

We are now considering vote No. 508, to provide for federal contribution to farm employment, forest conservation and supplementary pla-_ for single unemployed. The minister has indicated that under this item some million dollars will be spent on forestry work. I do not rise for the purpose of making any lengthy observation except to say that having sat patiently through the tirade, some of it just and quite a bit of it unjust, one would expect that the hon. member for Greenwood and his colleague immediately to the left would rise and say that this government is to be commended for at least one or two things.
I did.
The hon. member did. During the last week they blasted this government and they blasted the Minister of Labour, whose patience has been most exemplary, and they allow this item to pass.
It has not passed yet.

Just a minute. I listened to the hon. member while he made two speeches to-day, and perhaps I may be allowed to speak for five minutes without interruption. There have been severe critics of the administration, and I am not denying the merit of much of what has been said. If we would all approach this problem, not in the spirit of party jockeying, but in an attempt to get somewhere, more might be derived from our discussions. But when we do come to constructive items they arc allowed to pass unnoticed, and even the minis ter becomes modest in making any general observations. I think the committee might be prepared to listen to him at considerable length, telling us what is contemplated in this program of forestry work.
That is what we are trying to get.

The point is that the minister is prepared to do it, and I think he ought to receive from hon. members opposite cooperation and the kind of support he needs at a time like this. I am not rising in any political spirit at all, because with much of what has been said I. agree, but I do not believe we are going to get anywhere by making flamboyant speeches that are a combination of sincerity and political motives so mixed that it is not always possible to

identify where the particulars of the combination are to be found. I do think the minister might explain at greater length the forestry project, for example, which he announced the other day, to indicate not only to the committee but to the country at large how the government is meeting this problem. It may not be doing so to the full satisfaction of many hon. members, but still it is meeting it with a measure of adequacy having in mind the severity of the problem. The impression should not be left that the government is doing nothing and that it does not appreciate the problem which exists.

Would the minister tell us whether the item of a million dollars for forestry work which was announced in the press, and which the hon. member for Essex East mentioned a moment ago, is included in this appropriation or is it a special item?

In answer to the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Essex East, this whole item of S3,500,000 is intended to provide for special plans for single unemployed men. It includes 81,000,000 which has been set apart for the purpose of carrying out a national forestry program in Canada. That is not, I should point out to the committee, an entirely new departure, because under our youth training program last year, for example, we had some 2,500 young men engaged in forestry training, and that in turn is in addition to the forestry conservation camps in British Columbia, where between four and five thousand men have been engaged in this work during the past winter.
Under the proposed expenditure of 81,000,000 there is to be a division as between the work that can be done within the federal jurisdiction in our national parks and at our forestry stations, directly under the administration of the forestry service of the Department of Mines and Resources-that will take 8400,000-and then 8600,000 will be spent in cooperation with the provinces on forestry projects which are intended to be brought within the broad national program.
Have any agreements been worked out with the provinces?

We had forestiy projects under the previous youth training agreements, and this program is related, so to speak, from our experience gained in a more modest way, to the youth training program.
I think I ought to say to the committee that the day after the announcement was made I received letters from the Canadian Forestry Association and the Canadian Lumbermen's Association, both indicating that they believed this work was very much
[Mr. Martin.J
needed at this time and commending generally the action taken by the government in making possible an expansion of the work already done in forest conservation. I can only say that I hope very much that all the provincial governments will find it possible to match the amount set apart by the dominion government for forest conservation under the joint plan.

What does the minister mean by forest conservation? Where are these young men working? I have been over perhaps one hundred thousand miles of forest during the last year; I have searched everywhere to find where this work is being done, and I have found nothing outside the United States.

If the hon. member had been in British Columbia he would have found forestiy work being done in camps there. I have also visited the forestry camps in Manitoba, at Sandilands, for instance, and there is work being done in Quebec and New Brunswick close to the international boundary. I know that my hon. friend has travelled widely and is keenly interested in this work, but he will agree that it is quite possible to travel widely by rail, and even by motor, and not discover these forestry camps.
I mean by canoe with Indians.
If he wishes, I shall be glad to tell him where the camps are.

Is there not a forestry
camp within a hundred miles of this city?
At Petawawa, but that is a forestry station.
How many square miles in the dominion is it proposed to have this work cover?

I would be deceiving the committee if I posed as a forestry expert. The actual technical details will be supervised by the forestry branch of the Department of Mines and Resources. It may be that my colleague can speak with some authority on that point. Broadly speaking, the work will consist, first, of training by competent foresters with the object of fitting as many of these young men as can be absorbed into commercial forestry, and second, to do forest conservation work, the making of fire trails and so on.
Will there be any reforestation?

Some reforestation may also be done. We are quite agreeable to that being done in the various provinces. In fact, I am

Supply-Labour-Relief
told we have reached a point where it is becoming urgently necessary that thought should be given to reforestation. We used to think that the natural growth each year would repair the fire damage, but the experts are now beginning to realize that as a result of fire damage, and perhaps reckless cutting, many of our stands of timber are becoming more inaccessible, and that would tend to higher costs unless there was some reproduction of the forests.

Where can we find in
Ontario anything comparable with what they are doing in Kentucky and Tennessee in forest conservation? In those two states I found a great number of men cutting roads through the forests.
Fire trails.

Fire trails so that fire reels and teams and motor cars could pass through the forest quickly to put out a fire, but in northern Ontario I have travelled through many thousands of miles of forests and I have not yet found a fire trail. I have often thought that if a fire took place fifty miles north of the height of land when I was in the forest, there would be no way to get out and no way to get in, because I found no fire trails anywhere, and yet these were large forests.
The minister stated that the work would be done jointly by the dominion and the provinces. What proportion will be paid by the provinces?
There is an equal division of the costs under this plan. The administrative costs, however, are normally borne by the provincial governments.

I will not say anything about the motives he attributes to us, although I think probably our motives are just as sincere as his own; but I say this to him, that we have never withheld from the minister or the government any commendation which was due them.
But let us take the item to which the hon. member has referred, an item to provide for federal contributions to farm employment, forest conservation and supplementary plans for single unemployment. The total vote is * $3,500,000, and of that, $700,000 is a revote.

Just a
moment. The hon. member is asking us to stand up and cheer for someone feeding a peanut to an elephant. As I suggested yesterday, this is a penny-ante approach to a tremendous problem. Take one example. Take the farm placement scheme alone. The minister gave the figure a moment ago and I think I caught it correctly. He says that the total number placed in Saskatchewan under the farm placement scheme this year was 16,000. That compares with 26,000 last year.
The crop was that much better this year.
That is ground for satisfaction, is it not?

Just a moment. What were the rejections? Last year the applications were in the neighbourhood of
30,000,	and the previous year they were in the neighbourhood of 25,000. From my own experience I know that, in my constituency at least, there were more rejections this year than in any year that the scheme has been in operation. The regulations have been tightened up, and far fewer young men and young women were able to qualify this year than in previous years. I know of young people who qualified in previous years who could not qualify this year. I do not know who is responsible for these regulations, whether those administering the scheme in the province, or the federal government. I suppose it is by collaboration. But take regulation No. 2:
This plan shall apply only to the employment of an unemployed worker who is without means of support and in need of material aid as an individual, who is over the age of sixteen years, and who (a) has no home or established domicile within the province of Saskatchewan, and (b) or who, having a home in Saskatchewan, has been maintaining himself independent of such home during the period of at least one year immediately preceding the making of his application.
What happened to numbers of these young people? Some of them have been away from home; some have been on a farm placement scheme the previous year; some of them went out riding the rods during the summer months, working on farms in the spring months until the seed was put in, and by July they had nothing to do, so some of them went back home-	.
I see I have made a mistake.

-and disqualified themselves for becoming eligible this year.

I acknowledge that I made a mistake. I invited the hon. member to make another speech, and I should have stayed quiet.
I do not want the hon. member to lose any sleep about it.
I won't.

I am going to make the speech, anyway. I should like to impress upon the government that to my mind the regulations which were put in force last year defeated the whole purpose of the scheme they put in operation.
My hon. friend is surely going too far.

Well, it is certain that, for the province of Saskatchewan, to place sixteen thousand people under the scheme does not begin to meet the situation. Surely the minister must realize that while, in the early stages, to specify that a young man who was living at home could not participate in the scheme may have been all right, yet in view of the fact that we have had drought conditions and a depression for seven or eight years, and that these young people are growing up, the fact that they are living at home, and have not been away from home and self-supporting for one year, should not disqualify them. A young man has been living at home and helping his parents, but perhaps there are half a dozen sons in the family, so that he is not required; why should he not be permitted to go fifty or a hundred miles within the province to another farm and be hired there, just as a transient can be hired? They both require jobs. Sixteen thousand young people placed in Saskatchewan! There could have been placed forty-eight thousand in Saskatchewan had these regulations not been made as strict as they were.
I have received letters which state that applications have been rejected because the regulations specify that reengagement of present help will not be allowed. This is what happens in many cases of which I have personal knowledge. A young man who had been working under the farm placement scheme made a proposition to his employer when the spring came. The farmer said, "I cannot afford to keep you," but the man explained that he had no place to go. The farmer replied, "I will keep you until the crop; if I get a crop I will pay you, and if not, I will buy you some clothes anyway and you can get on the farm placement scheme next year." It was a choice between staying there and going on the road, so in many instances the young men stayed. But when

they came to apply in the fall they could not remain at that particular place because it amounted to a reengagement of help, so they had to move somewhere else and the farmer had to look round for someone else. That was particularly unfortunate in one or two instances where farms were being run by women whose husbands had died leaving them with families of small children. The widow had confidence in the young man who had been there the previous year under the farm placement scheme. Not having any crop, she could not pay him, but she bought him some clothes. This year his application was rejected and she had to let him go. While I appreciate what the minister has in mind- perhaps I put it too strongly when I said a moment ago that the regulations defeated the whole purpose of the scheme-
Yes, very much.

-for it did
place those transients who were eligible, yet it did not provide for the young people in the small towns and villages and on the farms throughout the drought area. I do not know whether the minister can grasp the situation. I cannot expect him to do so. He is here, removed from the problem. But in thousands of these little towns and villages all over the prairie there are young people who are not classified as unemployed because they are not on relief; their parents have a job, perhaps eking out an existence running an elevator for fifty or sixty dollars a month; they are living with their parents at home, and have been kept in that way for four or five years. They are not registered as unemployed, and no provision is made for them. Many of them went off to farms and worked during the winter. This year they were not allowed to do so because they had not been self-supporting for one year.
